title: Outer Sydney residents face higher car costs due to public transport scarcity
text:
When Caitlin Webster had her baby earlier this year, she could not leave the house for six weeks.

She lives in the car-dependent outer south-western Sydney suburb of Wilton, which is only serviced by one bus route that does not go near her house.

Following her caesarean section, she was not able to drive for weeks, leaving her housebound.

"I was going a bit crazy," Ms Webster said.

The Outer Western Sydney Alliance wants more investment in rapid bus routes. (Supplied: Outer Western Sydney Alliance)

"Even to get up to our local shops … It would take me over two hours to walk there.

" It'd be nice to just get out and be able to get on a bus to get out of the house. "

It takes Ms Webster 25 minutes to drive to her work in Narellan, a trip that would take 1 hour and 40 minutes if she took public transport using the infrequent bus service, a train from Picton to Campbelltown, then another bus to Narellan.

"I have no idea how you get out of Wilton if you don't have a car," Ms Webster said.

Public transport is limited in outer Western Sydney. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

According to the Outer Western Sydney Alliance (OWSA), just 12 per cent of Wollondilly Shire Council area residents have regular public transport within 400 metres of home.

In Wollondilly and Camden local council areas, residents live almost 9 kilometres from the nearest train station on average.

Car-dependent region residents spend thousands on vehicles

The scarcity of public transport in Sydney's growing outer west has prompted the group of councils to call for more investment in rail and bus infrastructure.

Penrith Mayor Todd Carney, who chairs OWSA, said residents were spending about $39,000 a year more on vehicle costs than inner-city residents and often lived in multi-car households.

Todd Carney says the region is spending thousands on private vehicle costs. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"We're looking to take over 30 per cent of the future population growth of Sydney into our region," Cr Carney said.

"We just haven't had that underlying infrastructure that's really required to make vibrant and really connected communities.

"For someone to go from the north of Western Sydney to the south of Western Sydney, you just can't do it unless you go into the CBD and back out again."

The OWSA said it expected about 38 per cent of Sydney's population growth, which would take its population beyond 1.4 million by 2046.

Cr Carney said the priorities should be funding rail and Sydney Metro links between Tallawong in the north to Campbelltown in the south via the soon-to-open Western Sydney Airport.

The Western Sydney Airport Sydney Metro line between St Marys and Bradfield is due to open next year; however, Premier Chris Minns has suggested it could be delayed until 2028.

North-west rail study en route

New South Wales Transport Minister John Graham said the government had invested $140 million into business cases for connecting the Sydney Metro from Tallawong to St Mary's and from Bradfield to Campbelltown and Leppington.

Mr Graham also said $302 million had been put into establishing five permanent new bus routes in Narellan, Oran Park and Mount Druitt, which began running in July.

The five services run between the new Western Sydney airport and the major transport hubs of Liverpool, Campbelltown, Penrith and Mount Druitt.

Outer Western Sydney will take on 38 per cent of Sydney's population growth up to 2041, according to the OWSA. (Supplied: Outer Western Sydney Alliance)

"Part of the problem is the former government's strategy of pushing all new housing development into Western Sydney without building the infrastructure to match," Mr Graham said.

"We're addressing that by making sure the rest of Sydney takes its fair share of new housing, and by delivering better public transport in Western Sydney."

NSW Shadow Transport Minister Natalie Ward said the Liberal-National Coalition had committed to expanding Sydney Metro and a new Western Sydney City deal to coordinate infrastructure delivery across the three levels of government.

"Western and south-western Sydney communities are suffering because transport investment has failed to keep pace with growth," Ms Ward said.

"Clearly more investment is needed, but the government seems more focused on spruiking investment in the Hunter than on south-western Sydney."

title: 3M lays out 'attack' on Commonwealth's $2 billion PFAS lawsuit
text:
US chemical giant 3M has shed light on its planned "attack" on the federal government's $2 billion lawsuit, which alleges the company withheld evidence that its firefighting products were toxic to humans and the environment.

The Commonwealth is seeking damages arising from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at 28 Defence Force bases across Australia and the areas surrounding them.

The largest-ever court claim brought by the Australian government alleges the company continued to make and sell aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) until 2003, despite knowing the dangers of its chemical make-up since 1979.

The 1,600-page statement of claim says the use of 3M's AFFF "resulted in significant contamination" of land and water, including drinking water, that posed risks to human and animal health and the environment.

Citing 310 internal company documents, the federal government's lawyers allege 3M falsely made assurances the product was safe despite having studies that proved variants of PFAS were toxic to animals, could cause birth defects and harmed the environment.

During a case management hearing in the Federal Court today, King's Counsel for 3M Phillip Solomon outlined what the defence's case would entail when it was filed to the court on December 11.

Mr Solomon KC said a "large team is working hard" and that it would "attack" the case.

He told the court that there were three courses of action it would plead to; public nuisance, a Victorian Environment Protection Authority claim, and a misleading and deceptive conduct claim.

Mr Solomon said the latter would need to be "delineated" between the overseas manufacturer and the local distributor of 3M products.

In its statement of claim, the Commonwealth alleges the company caused a public nuisance by interfering with the use and enjoyment of the environment and by hindering access to contaminant-free water.

Justice Catherine Button was told by the defence that the issue of public nuisance was not available in the matter.

"We will plead and ultimately contend that it doesn't contend a nuisance claim," Mr Solomon said.

"The allegation [is] that we had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that we were responsible for the special loss associated with the nuisance … and broadly had the ability to control the nuisance."

Williamtown residents in NSW have been exposed to PFAS chemicals from firefighting foam used at the RAAF base. (Four Corners)

The 28 bases have been split into three categories, including steady state, expanding, and in exceedence of Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and Australian Recreational Guidelines.

The Commonwealth has proposed that 3M plead to six "representative bases" that have features across those categories, including Wagga (NSW), Tindal (NT), Townsville (Qld), Oakey (Qld), Edinburgh (SA) and East Sale (Vic).

Mr Solomon told Justice Button the defence would be seeking to focus on one of the 28 bases in question, rather than six.

In reply, counsel for the Commonwealth Fiona McLeod AO SC said the Crown was "seeking representative bases" that covered issues such as cross-contamination, topography and soil type.

Questions over liability and toxicity

3M's AFFF firefighting foam was used by the Australian Defence Force for training and operational activities. (Supplied: CRC CARE, file)

The Commonwealth is seeking $2 billion to cover "substantial costs" incurred from contaminated land and water.

That includes $214 million for investigations, remediation and ongoing monitoring, and $367 million in settlements from five class actions brought against the government.

Mr Solomon told the court the case raised questions about allegations of toxicity and whether there was subsequent liability, particularly in instances where remediation had been carried out.

"When the Commonwealth cleans up bases … and sues us and seeks that sum of money … there are going to be questions [about] what, if any of that we would be liable for," he said.

The court also heard discussion about the definition of the term "potentially toxic".

"[The phrase] "potentially toxic" isn't a legal concept," Mr Solomon told the court.

"If [the Crown] mean to tell us that their reliance isn't really on a collection of words but a particular concentration [or] type, they can tell us."

Ms McLeod told the court the term was taken from the defence's own documentation and that it was for them to provide a more precise definition.

"There's no particular magic in 'potentially toxic'," she said.

Another case management hearing has been set for December 1.

PFAS is found in soils and water in areas where the firefighting foams were used or disposed of. (Supplied: Office of Lidia Thorpe)

When Attorney-General Michelle Rowland announced the legal action in May, a 3M spokesperson said in a statement that it had never manufactured PFAS in Australia and ceased sales of the products at issue about two decades ago.

"Despite this, the Department of Defence continued to use PFAS-containing firefighting foams for nearly two decades longer," it said.

Documents show Defence did not fully replace the 3M foam until July 2012.

title: Carlton suspends defender over drink-driving charge
text:
Carlton has suspended defender Wade Derksen for high-range drink driving on an off-season trip.

The Blues suspended Derksen for all pre-season games and up to round three of the AFL season next year.

The 25-year-old Derksen was charged with drink-driving in Jabiru in the Northern Territory.

Derksen failed a roadside breath test late last month, returning a high-range reading. His case will be heard in court in the Northern Territory next month.

Cowan suspended by AFL The AFL hands down its sanction to Lachie Cowan following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

"While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade's conduct falls well below the standards we expect," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions."

Derksen joined Carlton at the start of the season after GWS de-listed him at the end of last year.

He played 15 games for the Blues this season.

The AFL announced earlier today that Carlton's Lachie Cowan had been suspended for two games after an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

title: Sharing care for my son is hard. But I'm learning
text:
At 27, Dimity's son Stu moved into his own home.

Stu, who is autistic and requires substantial levels of support, has been living in the purpose-built house with 24/7 care for almost two years.

The transition has been an opportunity for independence that Stu craved, and a shift in responsibilities for mum Dimity.

But like for many carers, there is an invisible caring load that remains.

Dimity still recruits and trains support workers, meets regularly with a team leader, oversees Stu's support program, advocates for him and acts as his nominee.

"It's the hardest thing to do, to share that load. Even with other people in your family," 67-year-old Dimity says.

"To trust another person to take on that responsibility."

But Dimity is learning to share Stu's care with others.

These are her words.

We spoke to Dimity as part of National Carer's Week. If you'd like to share your experience of caring for someone, we'd love to hear more.

A determined young man

Stuart is my fourth child. I always say it was as if I had three children and then I got 10, because of the energy that he had.

He's an individual. There can be a tendency to think all autistic people are the same. And that is not true.

He has his own temperament and personality.

He is a very determined person. He is very perfectionistic, very focused. He loves cooking, crafting and creating things.

He micromanages; he observes. He has learned to knit simply by watching me knit.

On top of that, he struggles with issues of his autism: being non-verbal, illiterate, issues with emotional regulation, a need for predictable routines and rituals, problems with sensory overload, minimal social awareness, and intellectual disability.

Planning for the future

Dimity says sharing support for Stu isn't always easy, but she's learning how. (Supplied)

When Stu lived with us, it became apparent that, like all young men, he wanted more independence. He wanted to "divorce" his mother, as most sons eventually do.

It's the goal of every parent for children to reach independence; it was no different from my other sons.

He became resentful of my interference in his life.

We started to consider the process of creating a life for him where he had more control, more of a sense of agency over his own life.

Of course, in the background I still manage it, but it's not in his face.

In the couple of months prior to him actually moving, it was frenetic because I had a million ducks in a row.

I kept worrying that the degree to which this was working depended on me.

What would happen if his support workers weren't there? All sorts of worries started encroaching.

I actually had a medical event related to the stress, and from that time forward I started planning for a future of becoming somewhat redundant in his life.

I needed to work out how he was going to be supported when I'm not here. In a positive way.

Articulating my invisible load

Dimity also cares for grandchildren three days a week. (Supplied)

Now I negotiate a lot with the disability support agency we work with, working to expand their responsibilities and what they are willing to share. Also forward planning for Stuart’s future, including other people in his circle of support, like siblings and extended family, for them to share caring responsibilities.

I'm developing a working document that explains in detail everything I do as Stu's mother and advocate and manager.

When he lived at home, I was definitely like the boss.

Now I look to his care team to guide me, too. It's not just me teaching, guiding and managing; I'm part of the team, and we're learning together the best ways to support Stu.

I look after grandchildren for three half-days a week, on top of what I do with Stu.

It's busy.

As his mother, my job is to look after him. No-one else is ever going to love him like I do.

And while being a carer is a lot of work and most of my life has been devoted to caring for my children and now my grandchildren, that's OK. That's my job.

What I'm trying to work on by working with a circle of support, creating the working document, is the space for people in that circle to then volunteer to take on that responsibility.

The running joke is "If I end up under a bus, would you be willing to take on this role?"

While I cover it all now, there will come a time when multiple people need to cover it.

Our relationship has improved

I remember one night talking to my husband and deeply realising and feeling the loss of Stuart from my home. And really having a big cry about it.

That was hard.

However, my relationship with Stuart has improved vastly since he moved into his own home.

When home life is challenging, often overwhelming, it's easy over a period to start to diminish the degree you feel or engage in affection for someone.

To have relieved both of us of that has been such a gift.

Now when he visits, he sits next to me and holds my hand. He puts his head on my shoulder. He touches my cheek. He cuddles me.

I've always been devoted to him.

title: Family of man who died waiting for ambulance learnt of death through the media
text:
The family of a man who died in his Brisbane home, waiting two hours for an ambulance, only found out about his death through the media.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls said he was made aware on Monday of the 53-year-old Annerley man's death, which happened on Saturday.

However, he did not publicly address the incident until news reports broke of the death.

The man called Triple Zero (000) on Saturday evening, experiencing chest pains, and was asked, given his proximity to the nearby Princess Alexandra Hospital, to make his own way there.

Paramedics arrived two hours later and found him dead inside the home in Brisbane's south.

Mr Nicholls said the man's family were "disturbed to find out" of his death through news reports on Thursday.

"The family have reached out overnight and have seen the story in the media, and I think understandably are distressed about that, and I understand that.

"I apologise to them if that has caused them distress.

"One of the challenges that we faced was that the gentleman who passed away in Annerley was not known to Queensland Health and there were no contact details."

Tim Nicholls says he apologises to the family and hopes to address their concerns at a meeting. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The 53-year-old's family will meet with top Queensland Ambulance Service officials on Friday afternoon, and a review of the incident has been ordered.

A man in his 80s also died waiting for care on Tuesday, waiting for a bed at the Mater Hospital for approximately three hours.

"It is unacceptable, and I hope and expect that the critical incident review will provide us with answers as to how these circumstances occurred, why they occurred, and, of course, recommendations to improve the service and to address any issues that may be revealed," Mr Nicholls said.

The opposition in parliament on Friday interrogated when the health minister was made aware of the cases.

Review ordered after man dies waiting two hours for ambulance The 53-year-old man called for help after experiencing chest pains but was dead by the time paramedics arrived.

Mr Nicholls today revealed he was notified of the Annerley man's death on Monday.

"I immediately sought further information from the Queensland Ambulance Service as to what had occurred in respect to that matter," he said.

"Again, one of the challenges was that there was little information in relation to the gentleman's contacts and family details.

"I received a further briefing on Tuesday and was kept updated on attempts made to contact people during the course of the week."

He said the reviews of each death were underway and expected it to be a "fairly rapid process".

title: Teen killed in cricketing tragedy 'died by misadventure', coroner finds
text:
The grieving family of a 17-year-old boy who died in a cricketing tragedy say they are relieved a coroner will not recommend changes to the rules of the game their son loved.

Ben Austin was hit in the neck by a ball thrown with a side arm device while practising in the nets at Wally Tew Reserve in Ferntree Gully, in Melbourne's outer east, in October last year.

Cricket authorities confirmed at the time he was wearing a helmet but not a stem guard, which protects the neck.

Ben later died at the Monash Children's Hospital.

Coroner Simon McGregor on Friday confirmed the 17-year-old died as a result of misadventure by well-meaning young people using proper equipment at a "caring, well-run club".

Ben's parents Tracey and Jace wiped away tears as the facts were read at a directions hearing in the Coroners Court of Victoria, with legal teams for Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria also present.

Jace and Tracey Austin speak to media outside the Coroners Court of Victoria. (ABC News)

The coroner confirmed no adverse comments would be made about anyone's behaviour and "no individuals or organisations contributed to the cause of Ben's death".

He added that no recommendations or comments about rule changes would be made, paving the way for the summer cricket season to continue "in the normal way".

The coroner proposed commending the fact that some clubs and leagues had made safety changes without waiting to be told, with one bringing in neck guards and another banning the use of side arms.

But he said there was still some misunderstanding about individual clubs' ability to make safety changes, with some under the mistaken impression authorities would tell them what to do in response to safety issues.

The coroner is considering making a comment about the governance structure and how safety and best practice messages are conveyed.

The teenager's death shocked Ferntree Gully and the wider Melbourne cricket community. (ABC News)

Speaking after the hearing, Jace Austin said the lack of adverse findings and rule changes were exactly what Ben would have wanted.

"There's no way we want to change this great game," he said.

"But on the other hand, we don't want another Benny or Phil [Hughes, who died in similar circumstances in 2014].

"From what we've heard, it's exactly what we wanted."

With the anniversary of Ben's death nearing, he said the family would be coming together to reflect.

"Every day's tough, but when this comes to an end, this will be Benny's full stop, so you sort of want it to drag out."

"Every day's brutal to be honest."

Tracey Austin wore a necklace bearing her son's name.

"I've got him close to my heart," she said.

Jace and Tracey Austin say their family will be coming together to reflect on Ben's death. (ABC News: Wayne Hammond)

Cricket Victoria's Nick Cummins said the organisation would work through the coroner's initial comments and later findings.

"What we didn't want to do is go out and start finding solutions before we understood the coroner's findings," he said.

"Cricket is a safe sport. It's always been a safe sport. We have measures in place to make sure that's the case.

"But it's always important to have an open inquiry around incidents like this."

Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins attended the hearing on Friday. (ABC News)

He said the cricketing community had come together after Ben's death, with the Austin family raising $180,000 at a fundraiser last week.

"It's been incredibly heartening to see how cricket brings people together," he said.

The coroner's formal findings will be handed down before Christmas.

title: 'Investors freaking out' about Wall Street big tech as warning bell rings
text:
The cost of insuring against a big technology firm defaulting on its debt has soared to record highs.

These contracts are known as credit default swaps.

Heavily indebted data centre operator CoreWeave has been among the hardest hit.

Investors who lent the company money are now paying a lot to buy these credit default swaps to insure against losing their investments if the company defaults.

The so-called neocloud company has taken on more than $US50 billion ($72 billion) in debt.

The yield on CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 has hit 15.78 per cent.

This week, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps soared 16 per cent to a record 1.14 per cent, before easing slightly to 1.03 per cent.

Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu said the record highs in tech credit default swaps were an extension of CoreWeave's spreads blowing past 1 per cent.

"[It] has revived worries about how the AI build-out is being financed," Ms Wu said.

Turning to private credit

Wall Street's big tech firms are increasingly turning to debt and private credit financing, having exhausted options to raise money in the share market.

But elevated global inflation is putting upward pressure on interest rates, which is increasing the cost of this debt.

Competition for debt from governments and other big tech firms is also increasing interest rates, and the cost of servicing this debt.

Investors are increasingly concerned that debt costs are rising too much for big tech firms to service, and they are buying insurance to prevent harmful financial losses.

Ms Wu conceded financial markets were growing more anxious about these mammoth companies' financial health.

"Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended CoreWeave in Stockholm yesterday, saying its cost of capital is falling and it needs no Nvidia backstop, but I think investor sentiment on tech is fragile after the chip sell-off, so this is more sentiment than fundamentals for now," she said.

Elsewhere in the market cloud ⁠computing giant Oracle has seen its credit default swaps rise 0.3 per cent this week, while costs to insure against debt defaults for Nvidia, STMicroelectronics and SpaceX also rose sharply.

Credit default swap ⁠spreads for Amazon, Alphabet and Meta also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave.

Jensen Huang has defended CoreWeave's debt levels, saying its cost of capital is falling. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"This is not the first time we've had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, ⁠but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.

"AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."

Canary in the coalmine

Marcus Today senior markets analyst Henry Jennings described CoreWeave as the "canary in the coalmine" for excessive big-tech debt on Wall Street.

Wall Street risk signal flashing red Credit default swaps for US big tech companies are soaring to record highs. It means investors are fearful of a major Wall Street company collapse.

"[CoreWeave's credit default swaps show there is a] 60 per cent chance of default within five years," Mr Jennings said.

"Jensen Huang was quick to defend CoreWeave but then again, he is an investor and supplier to the company.

"Investors are freaking out on the cost of debt for wannabes," he said.

XTB research director Kathleen Brooks agreed.

"Its bonds have sold off sharply … this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions."

ABC/Reuters

title: Cowan handed AFL suspension following illicit substance investigation
text:
The AFL has suspended Carlton's Lachie Cowan for two matches following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

The league said "the circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public" were also the subject of the investigation.

Cowan was found guilty of conduct unbecoming.

He will be suspended for the first two home-and-away matches of the 2027 season and issued with a $5,000 fine.

Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne The club has confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward have been admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

No action was taken against Cowan's Blues teammate Will Hayward, who was also admitted to hospital on Sunday due to a separate incident.

Cowan's sanction was handed down as the AFL confirmed its new illicit drugs policy would come into effect in January.

The league said all players would be hair tested upon their return to training in January, "with readings going as far back as three to six months prior".

Cown said he should not have put himself "in such a vulnerable situation".

"I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club," Cowan said in a Carlton statement.

"I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was okay.

"This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this."

The AFL Players' Association (AFLPA) released a statement in the wake of the AFL handing down its suspension.

"This has become a public matter because private information regarding players seeking medical treatment has been shared," AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher said in the statement.

"That is unacceptable."

Gallagher said Cowan's suspension could discourage players from seeking emergency medical assistance.

"We don't want players using illicit substances and that is why the [AFL's] illicit drugs policy is so important, with its overarching purpose to change behaviour and minimise harm," he said.

"However, it is contrary to this health and wellbeing model to sanction players after they have sought medical treatment, particularly in an emergency.

"As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it."

The Blues said Cowan's wellbeing remained the club's priority.

"Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is okay and received the medical attention he needed," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake.

"Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward."

Lachie Cowan issued an apology via the Carlton Football Club. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Cowan will be required to undertake further education above the current mandated training on illicit substances and their effects.

The league said the matter would "constitute a notifiable adverse finding under the AFL's illicit drugs policy".

"AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations," AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said in a league statement.

"They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances.

"Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions."

title: Mayor says flood-prone airstrip may need to move despite $27m upgrade
text:
A flood-prone airstrip in the Gulf of Carpentaria may need to be relocated to avoid future disasters, despite a recent multi-million-dollar upgrade, the local mayor says.

The community of Burketown, 420 kilometres north of Mount Isa, had been without a commercially functioning airstrip after a "biblical-style flood" engulfed the region in 2023.

For the past nine months while construction was underway, the only way in or out of the region has been by bus on unreliable dirt roads.

The Burketown airstrip upgrades after major flooding in 2023 cost $27 million. (Supplied: Durack Civil, Jake Rich)

The $27 million Queensland and federal government-funded upgrade raised the airstrip by 400 millimetres, and commercial flights are expected to resume in mid-November.

Burke Shire Mayor Ernie Camp said while it was positive to see the upgraded airstrip, owned and operated by the council, back up and running, it should be moved to a more flood-resistant location.

"[Regular Public Transport] services are the lifeblood for small communities, aircraft aren't getting any smaller, and the number of people travelling on them aren't either," he said.

Ernie Camp has been campaigning for regions in the Gulf of Carpentaria to be more flood-resilient. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Although use of larger aircraft on Gulf routes could take years, he said planning ahead was key.

Cr Camp said he was a "little bit worried" the new airstrip would not survive another weather event like in 2023, but it was an improvement.

"It certainly has been an eye-opener in the amount of human resources and heavy equipment to come here because we had to totally rebuild that airstrip," he said.

"The tarmac had been compromised from not only the 2023 flood, [but also] the previous flood; the clay has certainly degraded."

Cr Camp said he had raised concerns with some politicians, but their suggestion was to "work with what we've got".

'Longevity' needed for Gulf investment

Western Queensland Alliance of Councils (WQAC) Executive Director Greg Hoffman said while he was pleased to see the airstrip improved and reopened, the challenge in the Gulf was to ensure assets have longevity and were not severely impacted by further weather events.

"The biggest challenge we have these days is to build sufficient resilience to get ahead of the game, so we don't find ourselves in five, 10 years having to do it again," Mr Hoffman said.

"[WQAC] has been very … in our advocacy to the governments to say that there needs to be long-term plans that take into consideration these potential adverse impacts into the future."

Mr Hoffman said investing to improve asset resilience was essential.

"Particularly in the case of Burketown and Gulf communities, the importance of air services and airports," he said.

"In the context of the importance of aerodromes in flood-prone areas, [Cr Camp's] argument has got a lot of merit [but] sadly, it will probably require a disaster to prove the point that what's been done at the moment hasn't achieved the objective of being flood-proof."

The RFDS and emergency services are crucial in Burketown, especially during the summer wet season. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The government launched a joint $119 million flood recovery package across northern and central Queensland after the 2023 monsoonal event.

A spokesperson for Queensland Emergency Management Minister Ann Leahy said the Burketown Airstrip was a crucial public asset for residents, and it was unclear whether the federal government's proposed disaster funding cuts would have delivered this project.

The spokesperson did not respond to questions about relocating the airstrip.

A spokesperson for the Federal Minister for Emergency Management Kristy McBain said decisions around the future location of the Burketown airstrip were for local council to consider.

"Under the [Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements], states and territories are responsible for determining whether a disaster is eligible for funding, and what type and level of assistance to make available to support recovery," the spokesperson said.

The Burketown airstrip was being repaired for about nine months. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

title: Sandalwood industry left in limbo as WA government mulls new rules
text:
Sandalwood producers in Western Australia say a lack of communication over looming changes to rules governing their lucrative industry has left them in limbo.

The native wood, prized for its use in perfumes, cosmetics and incense around the world, can fetch as much as $25,000 a tonne on the open market.

Sandalwood is one of the state's oldest export industries, dating back to 1844, and now a major cash crop in the Eastern Goldfields and Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Battye Library)

Under the current Sandalwood order, in place since 2015, 2,500 tonnes of wild sandalwood can be harvested annually.

But with that order due to expire at the end of this year, producers say the government has not been clear enough on what will replace it.

Sandalwood harvesting is managed by the Forest Products Commission, but new plans will restructure it under the DBCA.

Chief amongst their concerns is a proposed shift in oversight from the Forest Products Commission, the state's dedicated forestry body, to the larger Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), which governs WA's national parks and conservation estate.

Harvesters facing uncertain future

Michael Matthiessen says many are confused about how the transition to the DBCA is going to work. (Supplied: Mike Mathieson)

Harvester Michael Matthiessen got into the industry after moving to Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 600km east of Perth, 20 years ago.

While in favour of harvest reduction and a greater focus on regeneration, he said the shift to DBCA oversight had not been fully explained, and it was putting the industry in danger.

"I definitely think there's a risk to the industry if the transition isn't managed properly," he said.

"No one has been asking the questions to myself or other contractors that would give our perspective on the industry.

"And what is and isn't important going forward."

With sandalwood trees taking upwards of two decades to mature, Mr Matthiessen said harvesters needed to plan years in advance, making uncertainty challenging.

"It takes a lot of time, effort, resources and experience to be a really efficient and effective harvesting contractor," he said.

"Once it's gone, it's going to be quite difficult to recover."

Native sandalwood chips thrive in tough, arid environments. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

The ABC asked WA Premier Roger Cook about the industry's concerns and he said the government were stepping through the process carefully.

"We're consulting widely and doing some work inside the FPC at the moment just to make sure we've got the best settings," he said.

Exporters warn of international impact

Exporters share the on-the-ground harvester's concerns.

Wescorp Sandalwood executive chair Fleur Coakley said the industry was being left in the dark.

"FPC contracts are coming up to finish at the end of December, and none of us knows what's happening beyond that," she said.

"If it's not managed well and there isn't that cycle of investment going in … that's what my customers internationally are already concerned about."

Sandalwood oil can sell for nearly $2,000 per 100ml. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Ms Coakley recently joined a number of industry stakeholders, backed by the state opposition, to call for greater transparency from the government.

"Everyone's not sure whether we invest or whether we start doing plan B," she said.

"There's really no clarity at all and no formal announcement for any of us."

Ms Coakley is worried that the lack of clarity is creating uncertainty among investors and is worried about the impacts on the international market.

She wants the state to take a greater focus on illegal harvesting and regeneration.

"We've had different views, different approaches, and there's no continuity of discussing how transitions will happen or how this might work," Ms Coakley said.

"Having those different government departments, different ministers, it's really confused all of us."

Sandalwood heartwood can sell for $15,000 a tonne, but the slow-growing plant is considered vulnerable in the wild. (ABC Goldfields: Andrew Chounding)

WA Forestry Minister Jackie Jarvis and Environment Minister Mathew Swinbourn were both contacted to comment on industry's concerns.

Neither minister responded; however, in a written statement, a state spokesperson said a draft review was available and being reviewed by an independent panel.

"The Cook government is committed to facilitating discussion between interested parties to collaborate on what a future sustainable wild sandalwood industry could look like," the statement said.

The FPC and DBCA declined to comment.

Alternate models

Not everyone in the industry shares these concerns; Kalgoorlie-Boulder-based oil producer Dutjahn is one of the state's largest oil producers.

Director Keith Drage argues the industry has had time to prepare.

"Everybody's been aware that the current order … expires at the end of 2026," he said.

"Obviously we have very much a vested interest in what happens between now and then and thereafter."

Keith Drage and Darren Farmer from Dutjahn Sandalwood Oils. (Supplied: Jody D'Arcy)

Mr Drage said a transition away from government harvest on crown land to a mixture of independent Aboriginal operators and plantation resources was an inevitable outcome.

"We've always seen … that that was going to eventuate," he said.

"A diminishing wild harvest in Aboriginal hands is something that we've always built our business model around."

The most unexpected trend of the season is the cummerbund, with wrapped waists appearing at Celine, Valentino and Ralph Lauren alongside a host of indie brands such as Kallmeyer, Conner Ives and Mithridate. Here, the cummerbund sheds its stuffy, swashbuckling associations with rented formal tuxedos and ’80s pastel suits for a modern, genderless look. Stylist Jade Fox wears a vintage Gucci blouse and Harris Tapper trousers with a foam green lace offcut fashioned into a cummerbund. Sam Mooy The fashion item can be seen snatching in the waist of a slouchy sweater, adding structure to a slinky slip dress or adding heft to billowing pants. There are pleated cummerbunds, intricately beaded cummerbunds and jacquard cummerbunds – take your pick. As with most trends, this isn’t the cummerbund’s first go-around in fashion.

Advertisement

They made frequent appearances in the work of Yves Saint Laurent – accessorising a Le Smoking suit or adding definition to a brocade, drop-waist dress in the 1977 “Les Chinoises” collection. Jean Paul Gaultier, Helmut Lang and Anthony Vaccarello, among many others, all interpreted the accessory in their own ways. The name itself is an anglicisation of kamarband, an Urdu word (derived from Persian) meaning waistband. Typically woven from cotton, silk or wool, its distinctive pleats served more than just an aesthetic purpose, but could handily hold tobacco pouches, currency or ceremonial daggers. A Rajput Warrior, c. 1650, wearing a kamarband. Getty Images

Advertisement

London-based researcher, archivist and founder of South Asia Archive Sanam Sindhi, says locating the style in one specific time and place is difficult. “It’s an accoutrement that has long been in existence and exchange across many cultures in South, South West and Central Asia, each region with their own way of fashioning it,” she says. In colonial India, the cummerbund became a staple in British military officer uniforms, earning the name “cholera belt” as the thick fabric provided warmth and protection against the region’s harsh climate. “Though the British were eager to maintain strict sartorial boundaries between themselves and Indians during their occupation, the kamarband was one of the few items they did adopt into their own wardrobes due to its incredible practicality,” Sindhi explains.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Trends The $100 million fashion moment 65,000 years in the making “Taking it back with them to Britain in the 1800s, it eventually became the ‘cummerbund’, misappropriated as a signature of black-tie dressing.” Jade Fox, a Sydney-based stylist and writer behind Substack Consider This, was inspired after seeing the style pop up at fashion month. “The menswear Celine show was stunning. It was about blurring the lines between evening wear and casual wear,” she says. “We went through this phase of seeing a lot of oversized items with not much shape. And with the cummerbund, the waist is back.”

Advertisement

“It’s adding texture, volume and changing the proportion of something just by adding something to the waist,” says Jade Fox of the cummerbund. Sam Mooy Fox realised she had everything she needed to fashion her own cummerbund by raiding her arsenal of vintage silk scarves. “I haven’t actually bought anything new, and that’s one of the things that I love about the trend,” she says. “It’s adding texture, volume and changing the proportion of something just by adding something to the waist.”

Advertisement

Fabric remnants are another easy entry point. “I was wearing a pair of Levi’s blue jeans, a tee and a jacket, and then I just wanted to add something, but I didn’t necessarily want the harshness of a belt,” Fox says. “I have an offcut of an old Celine dress that I’ve tailored, and I just tied that around my waist. So it just took a relatively casual outfit and turned it into something a little bit more put together.” For Byron Bay-based stylist Doria Marque, the trend epitomises her ethos of sustainability. “One of the main things that I always tell my clients, is they don’t need to own a lot of clothes, or they don’t need to buy more clothes. I really like to focus on accessories,” she says.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Fashion Week The style lesson to borrow from Nicole Kidman’s Paris Fashion Week look For those looking to dip their toe in, Marque suggests visiting an op shop and looking at their scarf and fabric section (or getting creative with a tie). “Buy a simple one before you commit, like a classic black that’s easy to wear.” Though the cummerbund is rarely seen today in traditional Indian mens or womenswear, Sindhi says a new generation of South Asian designers are “reviving and revolutionising the way traditional dress is incorporated or adapted for modern, everyday style”. As always, fashion is cyclical and Europe turning its gaze east for inspiration is nothing new.

Advertisement

In recent years, other forms of South Asian dress – like the lahenga and mirror work (shisha) – have been recontextualised by Western designers. “What’s different now is that South Asians are more visible than ever before, have more of a presence in luxury spaces and creative industries, and more cultural authority that has empowered us to ask for accountability and acknowledgement,” Sindhi says. “India is a very tempting market opportunity for many luxury brands, with its growing economic power and wealthy clientele, but what should come with that is a desire to have a dialogue that feels mutual and reciprocal.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. title: Hero? Villain? Monster? Why DC’s latest leading man keeps us guessing
text:

As filmmakers build new universes out of iconic comic book stories, an inevitable crossroads is reached: to continue to mine what you know, such as Batman, Aquaman and Wonder Woman, or to step into something wholly new. The latter choice is risky. It paid off for Marvel Studios, which turned Guardians of the Galaxy from a second-tier comic book line into a blue-chip movie asset. DC Studios is making a similarly bold choice in following up its iconic Superman reboot with a story from the dark depths of canon: Clayface. Perfect? Maybe not. Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures The title given to this opening chapter of DC comic-to-movie stories is “Gods and Monsters”, a sign that the franchise’s creative lead, writer/director James Gunn, intends to put a very specific spin on the screen: after Superman, in many interpretable ways as a god, we meet Clayface, at first flush, almost certainly a monster. “What James Gunn and Peter Safran are building at DC is really exciting,” says 36-year-old Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, who is playing the dual roles of Clayface and his alter-ego, actor Matt Hagen, in director James Watkins’ adaptation of the story. “The notion of being able to have different worlds that have their own identity and their own place, on merit of storytelling purely, is admirable, and I have great hope for that to continue. How it all ties together is for greater minds than mine to answer.” Clayface – whose original name was Basil Karlo – was created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger for Detective Comics #40, published in 1940, and his creative DNA came largely from the early silent film era, and the canon of early movie monsters, such as Lon Chaney’s Phantom of the Opera, and Frankenstein, played by Boris Karloff. (Basil Karlo? The homage was hidden in plain sight.)

Advertisement

Something wicked this way comes. Tom Rhys Harries in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures Kane, of course, had created Batman, and was the author of some of DC Comics’ darkest canon. True to form, the original “golden age” Clayface was a failed actor driven mad when he discovered his magnum opus, a horror film titled Dread Castle, was being remade without him. “Whilst you have an awareness, as I do, of the long history of this character and the sense of responsibility and privilege to be able to bring that into live action for the first time, at a certain point, you have to take ownership over it and tell the story that you are telling,” Harries says. “So, [screenwriter] Mike Flanagan wrote a keystone blueprint that is the story that we’re telling,” he adds. “I would grapple with that to the point where I felt like I had enough of a hold of it that then I would be able to branch off and go back and look for inspiration or anything that might inform and aid the script that Mike had written. “That might take form and shape and many different guises, and it wouldn’t necessarily have to be the comic books, but it’s something that I was aware of. I continue to feel a real sense of privilege to be part of that lineage and to be able to bring that into live action for the first time … you are having a conversation in some way, shape or form with 80 years ago.” Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures At the heart of the story is Clayface’s face. Which is, at least at the beginning of the story, also Harries’ face. Until it is not. And at that point, Harries sits in a curious artistic juxtaposition: an actor, whose career is built, in many respects, off his face, playing an actor, whose face is disfigured, essentially destroying the man in the mirror.

Advertisement

“Something that felt really palpable to me on the first read of this feature was that Matt’s face is circumstantially important for what he has chosen as a profession, and the vanity of it doesn’t interest me at all,” Harries says. “It’s [more] like if a violinist lost his ability to use his hands. Or a film reviewer not [be] able to watch a film for whatever reason. “Separate to that, there’s an interesting by-product of being an actor potentially; that you then are commodified. And I don’t think it’s something that many actors that I know have a really complicated relationship with. Because it is just that. It’s a by-product of doing what my job is. “I don’t really know how I feel about it, to be completely honest,” adds Harries. “I have this sort of detachment to it. But I know that I love being able to collaboratively tell stories with people that I really believe in.” Loading In terms of building an origin story, Flanagan drew his inspiration from a two-part story from Batman: The Animated Series, titled Feat of Clay. The double episode introduced Matt Hagen’s Clayface, on television voiced by actor Ron Perlman, recasting him (slightly) as a washed-up actor dependent on a dangerous chemical to keep his face working. And notably, that television story opens with the image of the iconic masks of theatre that represent comedy and tragedy: Thalia, the Greek muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, represented by the laughing mask, and Melpomene, the muse of tragedy, represented by the weeping mask. The result is a curious contradiction: a character sprung from the superhero canon, with the footnote that he is, in essence, a super villain. But here, he has been reshaped by Flanagan, an accomplished director of horror television and cinema. Which leaves all of it in an uncertain and compelling space.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Cinema Woke but not broke? Superman soars above culture wars to dominate global box office “You’d be hard-pressed to find an individual who would be a self-proclaimed villain,” Harries says. “And I think it’s remarkable what human beings can do, and justify to themselves as actions. History is testament to that, as [are] certain things that happen in [the] present day. “To the point about the tragedy and comedy of everything, I’m constantly surprised by where humour comes from and how all of us are capable of finding the most inappropriate things or objectively wrong moments for laughter to come out of. I find that endlessly fascinating. “Part of the thing I love about him is his persistence and tenacity and strength of character that has existed way before we meet him at the beginning of this film,” Harries adds. “It’s also the thing that helps carry him over the course of the film. Whether that is expressed in the most ethical moral terms is not for me to say.” Another perspective Review What to stream this week: Josh Hartnett’s monster mystery, plus five more picks But what is left is a broken shadow of a man, whose heartbreak and rage allow him to be perhaps one of the most complex comic book characters ever written, either for the original comic book or as a cinematic adaptation. His humanity, however elusive, prevents us from wholly losing a link to him, and the possibility of a way back. “Real horror exists very close to the bone and something that is potentially deeply unsettling is when these fantastical worlds reflect real human characteristics and traits,” Harries says. “But also if you’ve had a great injustice done to you, then the response to that injustice is equal, and then the audience is judge and jury.

Pilbara miner PLS will fork out $1.9 billion after green-lighting the expansion of its Pilgangoora mine in the state’s north-west in a move that could see the operation become the world’s largest hard-rock lithium mine. The announcement is set to see the company overtake the world-famous Greenbushes mine in WA’s South West as Australia’s largest hard-rock lithium operation in terms of reserve volume, with a predicted output of two million tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate when it is fully operational in 2029. PLS produced a record 880,000 tonnes of lithium in the 2025-26 financial year. Tony McDonough According to PLS, the P2000 project expansion adds 23 per cent to the overall reserve tonnes at Pilgangoora, a larger current reserve, although at a lower grade, than at Greenbushes. The tonnage increase lifts the company’s ore reserve to 249.2 million tonnes at 1.24 per cent lithium hydroxide representing a 31 per cent increase in contained lithium.

Advertisement

PLS managing director and chief executive Dale Henderson said P2000 would transform the scale and competitive position of the company. “The substantial increase in Pilgangoora’s ore reserve reinforces the scale and quality of this world-class orebody and provides a strong foundation for the P2000 expansion announced today,” he said. “The maiden underground ore reserve is also a significant step in demonstrating the longer-term potential of Pilgangoora. “At 46.5 million tonnes at 1.50 per cent Li2O, it establishes a substantial higher-grade inventory beneath the existing open pits and provides further opportunity to create value over time.” Henderson said recent investments made in key infrastructure at the operation are expected to reduce operating costs, improve productivity and strengthen the existing operation, while also providing the infrastructure capacity required to support the increased scale of P2000.

Advertisement

The state government is supporting the expansion by investing $11 million to upgrade Wodgina Access Road, a freight route connecting Pilgangoora with Great Northern Highway and Port Hedland. Editor's pick Courts Pilbara mining company sues ex-employee over alleged secret breach Works will include a new intersection with Great Northern Highway and about one kilometre of road realignment, improving safety for all road users, including heavy vehicles. “We welcome the Western Australian government’s initial funding commitment towards the Wodgina Road upgrades,” Henderson said. “We have built a strong operating position at Pilgangoora and remain focused on continuing to improve it. These investments are another step in strengthening our competitive position and supporting long-term value creation through the cycle.”

Advertisement

The announcement has been welcomed by the state government and comes at a time when Premier Roger Cook has been facing increased heat over several key issues including child protection in the region. Cook said the Pilgangoora expansion would support about 1000 construction jobs, create 500 ongoing roles, and deliver new opportunities for local contractors and businesses across the Pilbara. “This is exactly the kind of investment that keeps Western Australians in work today and creates the jobs of tomorrow,” he said. “Every new mine, every expansion, and every tonne of lithium processed in WA means more jobs for Western Australians. Mines, Petroleum and Exploration Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the investment decision will strengthen WA’s position as a global leader in lithium production.

“As demand for battery minerals grows, projects like P2000 will ensure WA remains well placed to supply global markets,” he said. “Pilgangoora showcases the expertise, infrastructure, and investment environment that continue to attract major resource projects to our state. “Importantly, the project will expand employment and contracting opportunities for Traditional Owners and local communities across the Pilbara.”

The family of a Brisbane man who died while waiting more than two hours for an ambulance despite living just blocks from a hospital found out about his death through the media. The 53-year-old man called for an ambulance after suffering chest pains on Saturday night from his home in Annerley, a short distance from the Princess Alexandra Hospital. Operators called him back at some point and asked if he could make his own way to the hospital, but he told them it would be unsafe to drive in his condition, Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said. Nicholls said the incident is unacceptable. Matt Dennien They asked him to sit tight and call if the pains got worse, but about two hours after he called, the man was found dead by paramedics.

His call had been categorised as a code 1C, which are reached within half an hour 90 per cent of the time, according to Queensland Ambulance Service data. Aurum Resources is on a serious roll, hitting more gold, including a bonanza 0.65-metre intercept at 41.38 grams per tonne (g/t) gold outside its existing 570,000-ounce, 100-per cent-owned BST1 gold resource, ahead of a key resource update for the project due by the end of this month. The resource lies within the Boundiali South tenement at the southern extremity of the company’s flagship 3.22-million-ounce Boundiali gold project in Côte d’Ivoire, West Africa. The latest assays come from 25 diamond drillholes totalling 7121.75m at the BST1 deposit, as part of Aurum’s massive 150,000-metre diamond drilling campaign at Boundiali to test target strike and depth extensions and upgrade resource confidence. Aurum Resources’ massive 150,000-metre diamond drilling program, with 16 drill rigs across its Boundiali and Napié gold projects in West Africa, is expected to contribute significantly to the company’s upcoming resource update, expected by the end of October. The headline hit of 0.65m at 41.38g/t gold fell within a broader 9.55-metre section grading 5.18g/t from just 75.45m downhole depth. Other significant high-grade results - from three separate holes - include 1m at 43.93g/t gold from 268m downhole, 1.26m at 23.10g/t gold from a shallow 25m and 5m at 5.26g/t gold from 283m. Two additional holes also gave up 13m at 2.08g/t gold from 258m and 20m at 1.25g/t gold from 145m, including 6m going 2.29g/t gold. The drilling confirms the BST1 gold system remains open along strike and at depth.

Advertisement

‘Boundiali continues to grow in scale, and today’s results are expected to add to that.’ Aurum Resources managing director Dr Caigen Wang The results from this most recent round of drilling - including those still to come - will be incorporated into Aurum’s upcoming resource estimate, which had a drill collar cut-off date of 30 September and is slated for release by the end of October. The updated resource numbers will inform a definitive feasibility study (DFS) for Boundiali, which Aurum expects to deliver in late 2026. Aurum Resources managing director Dr Caigen Wang said: “We have received assays for a further 25 diamond holes totalling 7,122m at BST1, all drilled before the 30 September 2026 cut-off date for our next Boundiali Mineral Resource Estimate. These holes form part of the 120 holes for more than 31,000m (based on drill logs) completed at BST1 since the last Mineral Resource update, drilled to extend known mineralisation and to increase confidence in Inferred Mineral Resources.” Aurum is moving at a furious pace in West Africa, running 16 of its own diamond drill rigs across its project portfolio. The company is well funded for its aggressive exploration and development push, with an unaudited cash balance of more than $95 million following a recent $52.5 million placement. The flagship Boundiali project forms part of a 4.38-million-ounce combined gold resource base, which also includes the 1.16-million-ounce Napié gold project, also in Côte d’Ivoire, just 100 kilometres southeast of Aurum’s extensive Boundiali tenement block. The company plans to drill 30,000m at Napié, starting this quarter.

Advertisement

Both of Aurum’s key gold projects sit within the richly endowed and increasingly competitive Birimian Greenstone Belt, which extends over five contiguous nations in West Africa and hosts a plethora of multi-million-ounce gold deposits. The company’s ground lies in the immediate neighbourhood of major operations including Perseus Mining’s Sissingué mine on the border of Côte d’Ivoire and Mali, Resolute Mining’s massive 9.1-million-ounce Syama mine in Mali and Barrick Gold’s Tongon mine, also in Côte d’Ivoire, only 60km east of the northern end of Aurum’s 80-per cent-held BM tenement. With its fleet of company-owned diamond drill rigs generating core around the clock, a veritable mountain of cash in the bank and a resource update just weeks away, Aurum is not letting the grass grow under its feet in West Africa. The market’s attention will likely now turn to the next major catalyst – an end-of-month resource update that should reveal just how much bigger Boundiali has become after the relentless drilling assault on its already substantial gold endowment. Emerging gold producer Forrestania Resources has hit a series of critical milestones at its Edna May operation in Western Australia, putting the company on a fast track to restart gold production in mid-December. As a tangible sign of production readiness, the company has confirmed first ore from its Johnson Range mine has been delivered to the Edna May run-of-mine pad.

The company says its project execution risk has been materially reduced, with a new mill liner shipment underway for a late-November arrival and the first cell of its tailings storage facility nearing completion. Western Australia has a tightly regulated tailings framework, where new cells, lifts and substantial facility changes are subject to formal approvals, monitoring and risk controls.

Forrestania Resources is on track for a December 2026 production restart at its Edna May gold plant (pictured) in Western Australia.

While all eyes are on the imminent Edna May restart, Forrestania is also pushing ahead with its second strategic processing hub at Lake Johnston, slated for commissioning and production in early 2027. The company says key refurbishment and procurement activities are progressing well at the site, highlighted by the hot commissioning of the gold elution circuit, which is now underway. Other major components, including the motor control centre assembly and a locally bought conveyor, are in transit, while concrete works and screen tower refurbishment are also ticking along.

Forrestania’s restart timetable is emerging against a strong Australian gold backdrop with spot prices consolidating around A$6000 per ounce. That environment is supporting investment in restarts, mill upgrades and new production, with national gold output forecast to grow from 293 tonnes in FY2026 to 369 tonnes in FY2027, a massive increase of 26 per cent, according to forecasts cited by the Minerals Council of Australia.
