title: It’s the final weekend of Fringe – here’s what you shouldn’t miss
text:
Advertisement

This year’s festival has kicked off. Here, our writers take a closer look. See all stories .

CIRCUS

Na Djinang Circus | Ocker

Federation Square, until October 25 Five performers from First Nations-led company Na Djinang Circus navigate the crowd while delivering death-defying circus stunts in the middle of Fed Square. Na Djinang Circus show Ocker. Tiffany Garvie We turn back in time to a pre-colonial era as dramatic, otherworldly music plays in the background. The troupe roves through the crowd as if hunting, then gathers on a platform. The intimate audience of onlookers grows once the public realise that something is afoot. The choreography is dynamic, as the artists impressively run and tumble through people and across the stairs, doing lifts and climbing on one another. Embedding Indigenous knowledge in contemporary movements, performers emulate animals and cultural practices.

Advertisement

They cleverly introduce props – a ladder and a trolley – carrying and manoeuvring them across the flat and cobbled surfaces of the square. They mount the ladder, balancing on its rungs like a tightrope or handstand-style, then lay it on the ground like train tracks to ride the trolley over it, as if it’s a raft sailing along the Yarra River. Surprising and ever-moving, this place-based show is an exhilarating watch.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar Darby James in Little Squirt. Liv Morison CABARET

Darby James | Little Squirt

Ballarat Mechanics’ Institute, until October 24 In the depths of Melbourne’s lockdowns in 2021, Darby James clicked on a Facebook ad for sperm donation. The UK-born musical comedian premiered his one-man cabaret based on the experience at Melbourne Fringe 2023 as Spunk Daddy, and this week performed its 100th show at the same festival. Little Squirt is distinctly contemporary, wrestling with some of modern life’s heaviest dilemmas. Dressed as a seaman (say it out loud), James ponders the ethics of having biological children as a cis gay man, and what it means to have a legacy. The performer is a master of tone, somehow striking a perfect balance between ejaculation jokes and moving monologues, all with his tightly controlled vocals. The audience responds in kind, from raucous laughter to stunned silence. Tech issues on opening night mean that James is unplugged, adding an extra layer of intimacy to this already deeply intimate and thoughtful show.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

COMEDY

Creepy Boys | SLUGS

Meat Market, until October 17 This is Fringe at its purest – and this show comes with more content warnings than a film by Larry Clark. SLUGS was nominated for Best Comedy Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe last year, and rightly so. It’s delirious mayhem from Canadian artists S.E. Grummett and Sam Kruger. SLUGS is at Meat Market until October 17. Bokeh Media How often do you see the genitalia (some accompanied with googly eyes) of both performers, and see them threatening an audience member at gun-point, then offering another a very raunchy sex service that can’t be printed in these pages? Free candy is also extended to the crowd, so it’s not all R18+ (but it is 99 per cent of the time). There’s deliberately poorly performed puppetry (shout-out to a terribly voiced Joni Mitchell), and the two cosplaying as a horse. Essentially, it’s Play School on crack with a decent dollop of existential doom and dread woven in. If you’re a fan of comedic chaos with the capability of warping your mind, then I couldn’t recommend it more highly. If you prefer your comedy more middle of the road and TV friendly, then stay far, far away. SLUGS is a paradox of a show. It’s advertised as being about “nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing” but is somehow about everything. It’s breathtakingly stupid but ingeniously clever. I never want to see it again, but I also want to book again for tomorrow night.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

CABARET

Mara Knezevic | Kauboj

The Motley Bauhaus – Cabaret Stage, until October 11 In the hands of a master storyteller such as singer-songwriter Mara Knezevic, a simple tale about a Croatian man’s life and ambition becomes an enthralling and touching adventure. Two years after first staging Kauboj at Sydney Fringe Festival, the classically trained artist has brought her show to Melbourne. Kauboj by Mara Knezevic. Benjamin Draisma We hear about a chef-slash-cowboy named Jakov, who lives in the fictional Dalmatian town of Božje Selo. It’s a migrant story of hope and disillusionment. Through spoken word and song, Jakov’s world – brimming with purpose, love, fear and failure – is deftly and vividly created. Electric guitarist Daniel Potaczala strums along. Nostalgia and hints of humour are seamlessly woven in. Knezevic’s soulful, evocative vocals tackle a mix of traditional folk, covers and originals. Tender original tunes Till I See You Again and Cecilia’s Lullaby enchant, while we’re asked to sing along to an upbeat Kauboj Café and Grill. Professionalism reigns as stage lights flicker and falter and the sound plays up for a few moments. It’s a delightful hour that passes quickly.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio

Advertisement

THEATRE

In Bed With My Brother | Philosophy of the World

Meat Market, until October 3 Affectionately known as the best worst band ever, The Shaggs were a trio of young sisters from Exeter, New Hampshire, whose astonishingly inept songs were later reappraised as genius by the likes of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa. Philosophy of the World. Rona Bar & Ofek Avshalom That’s the official story, at least. Here, another trio reviews the legacy forced on three women who never wanted their spot in the limelight, but who were made to perform and record by a domineering father. In other hands, this material would lend itself to satire and condescension, but UK outfit In Bed With My Brother treats The Shaggs with respect while simultaneously trashing most conventions of respectable theatre. If you like your performances truly unpredictable, this is your ticket. Bristling with barely containable energy and randomly erupting into violence, music or comedy, the work suggests that to truly redeem artists with no aesthetic merit requires us to rewrite the rules of art itself.

★★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey

Advertisement

COMEDY

Stephanie Hare | I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy

The Motley Bauhaus – The Cellar, until October 18 From the outset, Stephanie Hare reveals their sleight of hand: physical misdirection and witticisms delivered with the gentle bemusement of someone almost surprised to find themselves delivering punchlines to an appreciative room. Adorned in a black funeral dress, the significance of which grows plainer as the show progresses, Hare moves from their sheltered, off-grid upbringing in Tasmania to a relationship that takes them to Scotland. Stephanie Hare, I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy. With a deftness that neither valorises nor romanticises a chronic illness at a time when thinness has been elevated to the pinnacle of feminised beauty, Hare traverses eating disorders, abortions and complex entanglements.

Advertisement

Hare’s tremulous voice belies a steady command of the room and their material. The subject matter is heavy, the revelations often harrowing and astonishing, but therein lies Hare’s talent. They’re exceedingly skilled at building narrative tension, drawing unexpected connections that make fun without making light, and delivering bons mots with a pin-drop precision that’ll have you simultaneously guffawing and grimacing.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair THEATRE

Hani El-Rafei | The Bruise

The Motley Bauhaus, The Cellar until October 18 What if instead of you fighting the pain, the pain was fighting you? The Bruise is Hani El-Rafei’s pain incarnate, and it turns out his pain has the form of a Victorian dandy. The Bruise is a high camp, richly intense character with a hint of buffoonery, and he takes centre stage while El-Rafei, relegated to a portrait in the corner, attempts to psychically wrestle back control of his mind and body. Hani El-Rafei in The Bruise. Through the retelling of a series of Arabian fables from his grimoire, The Bruise makes his case that pain is a worthy teacher. He asks audience members what they learned from the stories, and they are, of course, hilariously wrong. The Bruise entertains by deftly switching from the role of noble king to his jealous son, from gentle Layla to her mad lover, Majnun, and by cannily miming a menagerie of animals. It’s an accomplishment to make a show about pain safe, and wholly funny. The Bruise is the anti-hero we need to understand ourselves.

★★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu

Advertisement

THEATRE

Robbie Fieldwick | play.

Trades Hall, until October 18



Where does “play” factor in your life, now you are grown up? Has it been subsumed by sensible “adulting”, or do you still make space for unbridled creativity and connection? What even is play, anyway? In this immersive and interactive work, our energetic host reflects on a lonely childhood spent searching for a playmate, followed by a precocious young adulthood in which he discovered the “play” of theatre. Robbie Fieldwick in Play. Sarah Findlay Storytelling, theatre and physical games both new and familiar (chess, Lego, Jenga) are all employed to gently elicit answers from the audience. For Fieldwick, community is an essential ingredient, and by the end of the hour we’ve each shared something of ourselves and experienced a moment of connection with someone new. This feels neither forced nor daunting. Rather, it’s an invitation to consider the power and joy in the act of play, and a reminder that opportunities to do so are all around us every day, should we care to look and engage.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis

Advertisement

COMEDY

Anna Piper Scott feat. Margot Morales | Guillotine! or, A Modest Proposal

Festival Hub: Trades Hall - Quilt Room, until Sunday 18 October If this show’s description leaves you none the wiser as to what format it will take, there’s no easy answer. Rest assured, it’ll bring you this much closer to eating the rich. A performance lecture that debates the ethics of killing baby Hitler segues into a high-energy dance number which sees Anna Piper Scott and Margot Morales donning gauzy hazmat suits against a backdrop of capitalism’s excesses. Anna Piper Scott. Wayne Taylor The show is bedlam in a distinctly Fringe way. Scott and Morales constantly discuss their next move – the fourth wall is all but non-existent – which renders the show’s choose-your-own-adventure schtick even more fitting. Audiences are presented with three coloured folders with labelled flashcards, each symptomatic of the gradually escalating stakes of engagement.

Advertisement

You could be folded into a sketch that reimagines the exact time at which a certain propagandist is shot. You may be asked to inhabit a psychologist speaking to a comedian about the futility of employing art as “anaesthetic instead of medicine”. You might be treated to five minutes of stand-up on resisting AI. Scott reiterates throughout that she’s no longer a comedian, but her sharp asides and hilarious one-liners put paid to any doubt that she no longer is. Demonic right-hand woman Morales skulks around armed with a talent for memorisation, song and possessed dance moves. The show’s finale is Scott at her best – agitating, beseeching, elucidating – as she implores us to fight and endure.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair Death Club: A Brush with Death. Alan Robert Hopkins THEATRE

Jason Geary | Death Club: A Brush With Death

Trades Hall, until October 18



Imagine an intimate “paint and sip” session with a friendly Grim Reaper as your host. Ticket holders may bring one or two close companions into a dark, bunker-like room, which we soon learn is purgatory. I’ve brought my partner along for the ride. After learning of our untimely deaths, we’re invited to reflect on what we’ll miss most in life – then to visualise it through portraiture using crayons, textas and watercolours. If our host likes what he sees, maybe he’ll let us live. Geary as Death is both endearingly funny – he’d be right at home in What We do in the Shadows – and adept at reading the room to deliver a tailored and intimate experience. It’s an artful mix of comedy and contemplation, and I’m surprised by what the absurd exercise manages to elicit from us – both in terms of actual insight and the comically bad artworks we produced.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis

Advertisement

THEATRE

Hayley Edwards | The Carrot Show

Festival Hub: Meat Market – The Stables, until October 17 The Carrot Show is at Meat Market until October 17. Nick Robertson Staving off burnout, chronic illness and mental disquiet, Hayley Edwards is reaching outwards and within to find reasons to continue making art in a dumpster fire world. There’s their family lineage of puppeteers who’d visit hospitals to entertain sick children, which is incidentally Edwards’ very job. There’s their grandmother who finds joy in the quotidian details of the everyday. There’s their partner and creative collaborator Justin Gardam, onstage with them. And then there’s the beloved Carrot Man, Melbourne’s locally grown antidote to our dark, despairing times. A man armed with an oversized papier-mâché carrot skirting around the periphery of people’s visions to bring some unexpected joie de vivre to their day. Edwards totes their own papier-mâché carrot while dressed like one, as puppetry of incredibly ornate detail bears testament to the catharsis of creation – simultaneously functioning as a microcosm of our broader world and Edwards’ interiority. If the show occasionally veers into show-and-tell and suffers from a lack of cohesion, Edwards’ sonorous oration, natural comedic timing and beguiling manner ties it all together. Feel-good and life-affirming, the “carroting” philosophy of the show may just be the blueprint we need.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair

Advertisement

THEATRE

Liam ‘LJ’ Jumpertz | Best of Fringe Magic

Speakeasy Theatre – Apollo, until October 18 From a mind-reading giant white rabbit to an audience member’s ring reappearing in the most absurd of places, this rotating roster of magicians strikes the right balance between illusion and comedy. Featuring impressive displays of mind reading, card tricks and sleight of hand, the line-up is fun from start to finish. Best of Fringe Magic is at Speakeasy Theatre until October 18. Jayden Byrne Host Liam “LJ” Jumpertz – a talented magician in his own right – is particularly charismatic. He manages to foster an inclusive space for audience members, who he makes sure are comfortable and never pressured to participate (it’s “not that kind of magic show”, he explains). He is similarly supportive of the wider magic community, and the show provides a platform for a nice mix of established performers and newcomers. Jumpertz also pulls off some of the most remarkable tricks of the night, including a particularly memorable game of heads or tails that ended with a surprising twist.

★★★★

Reviewed by Gemma Grant

Advertisement

CABARET

Kelly Lim Harris | Yellow Fever: An Original Musical Cabaret

Trades Hall Music Room, until October 18 Yellow Fever: An Original Musical Cabaret is at Trades Hall until October 18. Maedforu The very title of this show is enough to strike fear into the heart of any Asian woman, triggering a cascade of memories of lecherous men. As Kelly Lim Harris sings in the opening number of her debut solo show: “It’s not a preference – it’s a case of yellow fever!” The New Zealand-born performer takes it further than just talking about her dating experiences, weaving literature, pop culture and cultural theory into the show, which becomes as much social analysis as personal testimony. There’s plenty of humour, but also real pain in these stories. Lim Harris’ classically trained voice especially impresses on a passage from Madame Butterfly, but is equally at home performing bombastic pop-rock originals – (Please Don’t Tell Me) I’d Be Great in Miss Saigon is a particular highlight. “We deserve to be represented with dignity beyond stereotypes,” Lim Harris says. This powerful show is not just for the Asian girlies – there’s something to learn here for everyone.

★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

WORDS AND IDEAS

Deb Robinson | In Her Footsteps: Women, Crime & Justice in Melbourne

Corner Fed Square and Swanston St, until October 18 While navigating the street-corner preachers, Hare Krishna dancers and evening hustle and bustle, podcaster and historian Deb Robinson provides a gripping guided tour about the women who have murdered and been murdered on Melbourne’s city streets. Robinson is quite the character in her bold Victorian-era hat. Many of the stories focus on victims and murderers from the 1900s: the murder of Linda Agostini, known as The Pyjama Girl; Alma Tirtschke, the victim of the Gun Alley Murder; and Jean Lee, a murderer and the last woman to be executed in Australia. Robinson delivers stories in a matter-of-fact tone with a touch of dark humour. Her knowledge of true crime is impressive, building a picture of the time period through archival photos and illustrations to provide context to these women’s experiences and actions, and hence the injustices committed. The session runs over time by 35 minutes (she notes that she’ll adjust this for the remainder of the run). Robinson considerately provides an exit point at the 90-minute mark for those who need it – though most remain. This tour is not for the faint of heart, painfully affirming that though these crimes occurred in the past, the attitudes behind them still remain.

★★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar

Advertisement

COMEDY

Clare Rankine | Inner City Glam Girl

Trades Hall – The Temple, until October 11 Inner City Glam Girl. Grace Neville Wake up babes, it’s time for pilates! Clare Rankine is Inner City Glam Girl: a self-flagellating content creator-cum-Kookai manager-cum-pilates instructor. She needs this class more than you do, because she had 11 espresso martinis at Revolver last night. Don’t be late or she’ll charge you the late fee, and the admin fee, and the credit card fee. Rankine’s stellar performance is more akin to full-on demonic possession, head almost whipping 360 degrees to follow you with her vacant eyes and frozen smile, as she pulses and sweats on the reformer machine. You’ll laugh so hard it hurts. And in pilates, if it hurts, push harder! ICGG is a woman on the brink of a physical, emotional and spiritual breakdown. Rankine’s writing is brilliantly restrained, and there’s just the right amount of audience participation. If you’ve ever wondered what was wrong with the pilates princesses, Rankine will show you.

★★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu

Advertisement

EXPERIMENTAL

Rebekah Carton | Everything, Now!

The Motley Wherehaus, until October 11 Everything, Now! Matto Lucas If you’ve ever felt your to-do list growing faster than you can cross items off, this manic-paced experiment in optimism will have you on board from the outset. Armed with an extensive toolkit and bottomless reserves of energy, Rebekah Carton is charged with a series of random challenges from a seemingly endless list. They range from the mundane (decorate a cake) to the infuriating (untangle fairy lights) to the abstract (make a new friend). To say that they come thick and fast is an understatement: imagine a season of Taskmaster crammed into 45 minutes. A pulsing electronic soundtrack and an oversized digital countdown add to the sense of time running out. Carton is a hugely relatable presence: whether you’re a gig worker, a young ’un navigating hustle culture or a parent juggling constant demands, this entertaining encounter will provide a shot of catharsis and a reminder that you’re not in this alone.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey

Advertisement

DANCE

Ngioka Bunda-Heath | Estuary

Northcote Town Hall, until October 10 The river is within us, the sea is all about us: this is an unpretentious but involving study of the patterns and rhythms of water, a short, strikingly presented duet – danced by Brooklyn Bond and Jack Sheppard – travelling upstream from coast into country. Estuary is at Northcote Town Hall. Luke Currie-Richardson The performance area is defined by a square of video projected onto the floor. At first, we see an expanse of swirling sea. The dancers hold still, vertical poses, feet thrust skyward, as though arrested mid-plunge into the restless blue and white. Nearer the coast, they roll and tumble up and down the stage, like waves breaking and receding. Further inland, as the stream narrows, we see long chains of phrases, quickening, assembling varied gestures – like surface reflections of the life that surrounds the river. As the work progresses, the space narrows and the action accelerates: it’s a simple but compelling device. The material never feels overworked and the dancing is light and attractively loose. A charming evocation of place from a First Nations perspective.

★★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSICAL

Girlhood Productions | Girlhood in the Bathroom

Explosives Factory, until October 17 Girlhood in the Bathroom is at Explosives Factory until October 17. Josh McClure It’s New Year’s Eve and two groups of friends – besties Steph (Imogen Brown) and Gwen (Sarah Eaton), and lifelong trio Kiya (Amaya Pardillo), Baylee (Alice Quick) and Zoe (Hannah Manderson) – meet in a club bathroom. They may be strangers, but soon the girls are sharing all their secrets and fears, soundtracked by upbeat pop bangers and choreography to boot. Created by its five young stars, Girlhood is both self-assured and irreverent. Exaggerated theatrics elevate a hammy rap and the hilarious song F--- Men, complete with doo-wop harmonies, show there are hints of the musical sitcom Crazy Ex-Girlfriend here. The production balances humour with vulnerability. Clever choreography depicts the trauma of sexual assault; the stage becomes a choral confession booth. Props and staging are minimal, embodying the claustrophobia of the bathroom and the girls’ minds. Both thematically and musically, the show is slightly overstuffed, and some harmonies are askew – but the cast’s charm and chemistry make this debut a blast.

★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

COMEDY

Caitlin Duff | Freidah Will See You Now

Trades Hall, until October 18 Freidah Will See You Now is at Trades Hall until October 18. Charlie Ashfield Welcome to the show! Unfortunately, you’re dead. Even worse, you’re in the netherworld. Please form an orderly queue as we wait for the boat to cross the River Styx. Freidah will accompany you when the transport is ready. Caitlin Duff’s solo clowning debut has just won them the Best Comedy at the Sydney Fringe, following a Best Newcomer and Golden Gibbo nomination at this year’s Melbourne Comedy Festival. It will come to a surprise to no one that Duff’s an alum of Ecole Philippe Gaulier’s illustrious French school. Dressed up to the nines, they’re in make-up and costume to suit the occasion. Their hatred towards men and their deserving of a place reserved in Hell is apparent from the get-go: “Where are the men? Identify yourselves!” they screech. A few nervous audience members put their hands up. “You’ll fall in the river now, she doesn’t take kindly to trash! Just a little light misandry doesn’t hurt, it helps us build community.” The following 40 minutes have Freidah entertaining us in purgatory before we enter eternal damnation. The idiom of having an audience eating out of your hand is surpassed. Their improvisational skills are also impressive, proved by an audience Q&A handled deftly and garnering some of the show’s biggest laughs. When the boat finally arrives and the lights go out, the audience moan as they want more. If this is death, then my existential dread for the past two decades has been thunderously unnecessary.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

COMEDY

Steph Crothers | Daddy Daycare

Trades Hall, until October 17 Having worked as both a children’s entertainer and a stripper, Steph Crothers has one of the more distinctive comedic voices on the circuit. She’s combined the two to create the scorchingly feminist show Daddy Daycare, where she plays a sickly sweet but hypersexual daycare teacher to help grown men achieve their government mandated “Working With Women’s Check”. The one lesson to pass? How to interpret, respect and enact the boundaries of consent. Daddy Daycare is at The Motley Bauhaus until October 17. Nick Robertson The set design is straight out of Play School. There are erogenously shaped windows to look through, sexual approval games to play and educational toys (Crothers transforms into an animatronic sex doll). A pleasure-deprived puppet vagina engages the crowd in a sing-along explaining the anatomy of the female reproductive system and teaches them about sensual areas, plus a striptease version of Hokey Pokey teaches an audience member himself when to say “no”. Whoever you are, there’s a good chance you will end up face-to-face with Crothers’ derrière – but that is, only if you consent. It’s smut for the sake of essential sexual education. Unfortunately, at times, it feels like preaching to the converted. It will no doubt aggravate members of the manosphere and see them rebuff the concepts (on the opening night a series of outbursts led to a man being kicked out). They’re undoubtedly the ones who need to see it most – especially the volcanic finale which details disturbing encounters that inspired the creation of the show. Maybe Crothers could send a copy to the Tate brothers to entertain themselves while they remain in prison to start the conversation?

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

THEATRE

Bron Batten | Waterloo

Trades Hall, until October 18 Bron Batten’s multi-award-winning tale of curdled romance premiered in 2019 but has only grown in relevance since. Waterloo is at Trades Hall until October 18. Theresa Harrison The “lefty, Greens voting” artist wasn’t exactly looking for love in all the wrong places (we’re talking Paris, c’mon) but it was a sacre bleu! moment when she realised her new beau was a hard right conservative whose military exploits made newspaper headlines. What begins as a dating-the-enemy comedy slowly transforms into something more complex, however, as Batten makes clear that the fog of war applies to skirmishes of the heart, too. There are no clear battlelines here, though there are plenty of solid laughs. In the end, Batten’s willingness to confess to her vulnerabilities and lay bare the messiness of l’amour fou are an antidote to the polarisation and quick condemnation of contemporary discourse. All’s fair, as they say, even when Batten realises the game was rigged from the outset.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey

Advertisement

COMEDY

Bahaa Dabbagh | A Lucky Refugee?

Wheat, Wine & Whisky, until October 11 Bahaa Dabbagh escaped a Syrian civil war zone where he once spent 14 hours hearing seven missiles a minute deployed over his community. Softly spoken and nuanced, laughs flow freely as he conjures material from the darkest of places in his sophomore solo show. Beginning with tales of his origins, he details running to work through the Syrian streets while dodging snipers, alongside being arrested multiple times and inflicted with psychological torture when the revolution came. A Lucky Refugee? Paul Dunn Joined by Sasha, his newly adopted feline partner in escaping war crimes, Dabbagh made a cross-continental journey to Australia via Turkey. On the way he gambled his life with a gun to his head to save Sasha’s seat on a bus, and she repaid the favour by saving him from prison and military conscription. Anecdotes of having to prove his relationship to his then-girlfriend is real to obtain a visa, coming to a literal crossroad during warfare and juxtaposing it against Australian politics, and explaining why he believes war in the Middle East is so prevalent due to sex-related frustration all land soundly. But it’s his final line, declaring why he doesn’t want to be the voice for all refugees, that might be the best joke of the festival. Alongside his fledgling comedy career, Dabbagh has always used creative endeavours (advocating, fundraising and teaching Syrian cuisine to locals via cooking classes) to breathe new life into the stories of those who have been displaced. Their loss is our gain.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

DANCE and PHYSICAL THEATRE

Emma J. Hawkins and Leisa Prowd | Exhibit

La Mama Courthouse, until October 4 Two short-statured women walk on stage, inviting the audience to stare. But how do we see them? Is it with the weight of the caricatures and tropes that come with bodies their size on a stage, or as they see themselves? It offers a range of performers delivering a taste of what they offer, leaving the audience hungry to seek them out elsewhere at the festival. The featured comedians hail from all over the country, and with a mix of four performers each night there is a satisfying variety of styles.

Advertisement

When I attended, Wiradjuri/Kamilaroi performer Jacob Keed opened with a laconic storytelling style to ease the audience in, followed by Gamilaroi comic Ben Moodie. His material skewed darker with quick jabs that met their mark. Ngarrindjeri actor/producer/comedian Kimmie Lovegrove’s personal material offered a tempting preview of the material in her solo show, which will open later in Fringe. Kamilaroi performer Cameron Ribbons, the MC for the evening and the closing act, stole the show on this night by hitting a sweet spot of storytelling and punchy jokes. His re-enactment of crocodile spotting was the perfect crescendo.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton DANCE

Weichen Cui | In Green, In White

Dancehouse, until October 3 The Chinese folk legend of Lady White Snake is forever shedding one skin for another. The most recent retellings shift the focus from White Snake’s mortal lover to her demonic servant, Green Snake, recasting the bond between mistress and maid in terms of enduring female friendship and homoerotic desire. In Green, In White. Georgia Moloney

Advertisement

Choreographer Weichen Cui explores this queer transformation in a new duet with Jiawen Feng. At first, the performers are silhouetted behind separate screens, isolated, wearing costumes informed by tradition. As if reflecting the evolution of the story, the two figures are gradually brought together – culminating in a final serpentine tangle of limbs. There are interesting moments, such as the use of waacking to playfully disrupt a fan dance. But overall, the episodic structure feels slow and over-formal, arresting the flows of desire it seeks to release. It might also be a little long – compressed to half an hour, this duet could bring its strongest moments into more volatile contact.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann DANCE

Joyce Liu | INTERLINK_SYSTEM

Dancehouse, until October 3 Joyce Liu stands before us in the gloom, a tangle of red wires trailing from one arm, fingers twitching. Finally, we get it: she is actually controlling the soundscape, summoning jackhammer bursts and ominous bass drones from a body that barely seems to move. As the noise intensifies, four creatures wake inside a plastic greenhouse behind her. They claw at its walls, tearing them open. Free at last, the juddering young humanoids – all in their underwear – begin feverishly coupling in a sort of grotesque orgy-of-Doctor-Moreau. INTERLINK_SYSTEM. Carlin Stephenson

Advertisement

Liu – also director and choreographer – builds a convincingly creepy laboratory atmosphere, with smoke and wildly sweeping lights lending urgency to the action. There’s also some irony, even comedy, in the monstrous debauch – though it does go on and on. I do think, however, we could have stayed with that opening image of the human wired for sound a little longer, perhaps giving the idea of an interlinked system more room to unfold – before rushing into the bioengineered bacchanal.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann THEATRE

Ben Grant | Wrong Way, Grow Back

La Mama Headquarters, until October 18 Wrong Way Grow Back channels long-time actor, Ben Grant’s warm-hearted charm and boyish sincerity for a part-stand up, part-confessional reflection on family lineage, memory, and grief. The title names Grant’s stop-and-start style of delivery, as he swings from mournful anecdotes about his parents’ meet-cute at Harvard to light-hearted stand up about the romance of letter-writing.

Advertisement

Ben Grant in his Melbourne Fringe Festival show Wrong Way, Grow Back. Darren Gill He’s an endearing performer. But the show lacks focus. Though the scattershot logic of Grant’s stream-of-consciousness style has an occasionally charming unpredictability (an uncanny Louis C.K. impression notwithstanding), it’s too much to ask even the most game audience to go from twee word play to sermonic political rants with nothing but the refrain “Why was I telling you this?” to justify the diversion. If there’s a chaotic appeal to Grant’s jarring transitions, it comes at the expense of the simple effectiveness of moments when he draws from his talents as a dramatic actor to deliver something closer to the intimate style of confessional or verbatim theatre: whether quietly reading from his parents’ letters to each other, or choking up when he tries to make a joke about his mum. The simplicity of these moments of quiet vulnerability stripped back the clutter to present a process of painful remembrance unique to grief, where two lines on an old letter can stop time and let you ‘grow back’. At least for a moment.

★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster COMEDY

Gill Cordiner, David Callan and Iain Pringle | 100% Scottish Comedy

Elephant and Wheelbarrow, until October 16

Advertisement

100% Scottish Comedy is at Elephant and Wheelbarrow until October 16. Brian Taylor Three Scottish stand-ups pull a decent-sized comedy-seeking crowd for a Monday night. There are 30 or more people thirsty for a laugh at the bustling inner-city pub. David Callan welcomes “Monday drinkers” before launching into a diatribe about how crappy Perth is. He seeks validation from the crowd, revealing he’s trialling new bits. While some chuckles surface, many quips and observations get the silent treatment. Next is Iain Pringle, whose attempts at an Aussie accent elicit mild mirth. Again, Perth is bagged out. After the half-way mark, he notes, “I’m definitely losing you on this”. Ramblings about working for the NDIS entertain some. Gill Cordiner’s fun crowd banter leads to light-hearted ribbing of prime targets – a bald bloke, a man wearing a hat indoors and a younger fellow with facial hair. Oddly, there’s even more rubbishing of Perth. A highly relatable dig at Melbourne’s foodie scene gets the biggest laugh of the night.

★★

Young cricketer Ben Austin died by “misadventure”, a coroner investigating the 17-year-old’s death has said. Just weeks from the first anniversary of Ben’s death, his parents, Jace and Tracey Austin, attended the Coroners Court of Victoria on Friday for a brief directions hearing. Junior cricketer Ben Austin died in a training accident on October 28 last year. Ferntree Gully Cricket Club Coroner Simon McGregor revealed he would not be making any adverse findings or recommendations about the circumstances surrounding the incident. He said no individual or organisation had contributed to Ben’s death, and it was “a misadventure by well-meaning young people using proper equipment, using equipment that was proper, using it properly, in a caring well-run club”.

Advertisement

Ben died in hospital after being hit in the neck by a ball, thrown by a teammate using a side arm ball-throwing device, while training in the nets in Ferntree Gully, in Melbourne’s south-east, before a scheduled T20 game on October 28 last year. On Friday morning, Ben’s parents both cried silently, holding hands, as the counsel assisting the coroner read a summary of the events of that day, including that Ben’s teammate initially thought he was “mucking around” before realising it was serious and calling over the senior coach, who began performing CPR. Ben’s parents Tracey and Jace Austin outside the coroners court. Wayne Taylor Paramedics arrived and took the teenager to Monash Children’s Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead. A post-mortem examination concluded Ben had likely died from an intracranial haemorrhage, or brain bleed, resulting from a tear to a major neck artery caused by traumatic injury. McGregor said the way Ben had died was “a very rare but not unknown occurrence”, citing two or three other similar incidents in the past 12 years, but he felt confident Cricket Victoria and Cricket Australia were reviewing a range of measures to make the game of cricket safer, including new technologies and helmet design.

Advertisement

“For cricket administrators and clubs, though, I do want to share and give you comfort that there will be no recommendations or comments made here about rule changes … and the cricket season that’s upon us can continue in the normal way.” Related Article Updated

Tragedy ‘Here we go, lads’: The radiant life and tragic death of a beloved Gully boy Outside court, Jace and Tracey Austin, who was wearing a necklace with Ben’s name on it, said they were comforted to learn there would be no changes made to the game their son loved. “From what we’ve heard, it was exactly what we wanted,” Jace Austin said. “In no way did we want to change this great game. It was a freak accident.” While the coroner said he was only a couple of weeks away from finishing his investigation, he offered to leave some space for Ben’s family to observe the looming anniversary of his death, which they accepted. Final findings are expected before Christmas.

Advertisement

“Every day’s tough. But again … when this comes to an end, this will be Benny’s full stop, so you sort of want it to drag out,” Jace said. “We had his 18th last week, and now we’ve got his anniversary coming up. So, but every day’s brutal. I’ll be honest, every day’s brutal. “He was just a shy little 17-year-old boy … who just wanted to go about his life … I still can’t believe how many times he’s been on the front page of the news. Jace and Tracey Austin speak after a coroner said their teenage son Ben died by “misadventure”. Wayne Taylor “It’s been quite amazing to be honest … We were worried that he’s going to be forgotten, but he’s going to outlive us all.” Reviews are still in train across Cricket Victoria and Cricket Australia into broader governance and the way potential safety risks are communicated, which the coroner said was one area he felt needed work, identifying some confusion among clubs as to whose responsibility it was to enforce safety-related rule changes.

Advertisement

McGregor commended the fact that some clubs had taken proactive action, with Laurimar Cricket Club bringing in neck guards for all players and Ferntree Gully Cricket Club banning the use of sidearm ball-throwers. But he said other clubs seemed to be waiting to be told, despite Cricket Australia saying it could only make strong recommendations, and had, but could not force lower leagues to implement changes. Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins told reporters outside court that cricket was a safe sport, but that it was important to investigate all serious incidents thoroughly. He said the cricket community was still mourning the teenager’s death. “We will continue to support [his family] and ensure that Ben is never forgotten,” he said. Ben’s death triggered an outpouring of grief across the local, domestic and international cricket communities.

The Austin family have set up a charity – the Ben Austin Legacy – to help other families going through loss. His father said it had helped him and Tracey stay united in grief.

Advertisement

“School-age loss causes a lot of grief on a marriage. It doubles the divorce rate, and I get it … Everyone grieves their own way, but now, I think, working on Benny’s gala, Benny’s legacy, we’ve really come together and ... we’ve also got two other boys, who are 16 and 13, and that they need us as much as anyone.” Jace Austin said both boys were still playing cricket, and he was still watching them play whenever he could. “Friday night, Saturday, and Sunday still. I take my dog Marley down … I just need to. It helps me so much,” he said. “Benny would be overwhelmed by all this stuff to be honest, all this hype. He was just a bit more like his mum, a little bit more reserved … He was the perfect boy … He would have just wanted the game to go on … and I hope that we get the message out of here. title: 'Asymmetrical social warfare': Kelly Clarkson, a mechanical bird, and store put 'in danger'
text:
In Brief A dispute over a mechanical bird has snowballed after duelling claims and accusations of online harassment.

A New York toy shop says Kelly Clarkson's complaints sparked abuse and put staff "in danger".

A singing mechanical bird named Molly has become the unlikely epicentre of a public dispute between singer and television host Kelly Clarkson and a small novelty store in New York.

What began as a shopping trip to a Brooklyn toy and magic shop has since escalated into a fight involving competing Instagram statements, leaked CCTV footage, accusations of online harassment, and claims staff have been put "in danger".

It's also, somehow, left the world's "most famous" singing bird with a new US$15 million ($21.4 million) price tag.

The saga began when Clarkson visited Art of Play — a toy, games and magic shop in Brooklyn.

Among the items on display was Molly, a handcrafted singing and dancing animatronic bird mounted on a wall inside the shop.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Not long after leaving, the Grammy-winning singer made a post on X claiming she'd felt judged by staff while trying to make a purchase.

"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it," Clarkson wrote.

Clarkson compared the experience to a famous scene from the film Pretty Woman, in which Julia Roberts' character is dismissed by sales assistants in an upmarket boutique.

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said.

Kelly Clarkson's visit to a Brooklyn toy and magic shop has sparked a viral dispute over an animatronic bird.

At the centre of the disagreement was Molly, which Clarkson says she wanted to buy despite the item's US$15,000 ($21,400) price tag.

"[I] was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson said.

"Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale."

Molly 'not for sale', store says

Art of Play disputed Clarkson's version of events and said there had been a misunderstanding.

In a statement posted on Instagram, the store said Molly was never available for purchase because she served as a mascot and fixture of the store.

"Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale," the store said.

The store later expanded on that explanation, saying staff told Clarkson that, while Molly was not for sale, a similar bird owned by the automaton's creator, Seattle artist Bliss Kolb, could potentially be purchased for US$15,000.

Art of Play also said staff offered to show Clarkson another mechanical bird made by a German clockmaker that sold for about $2,000 ($2,860)

"She did not stick around long enough to see it," the business said.

Clarkson subsequently disputed that account, saying staff had explicitly told her Molly was for sale.

"So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale while pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator-eyed me saying in a condescending tone, 'Yes, it’s for sale, but it costs $15,000 so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you, I can'," she wrote on X.

Clarkson said she regularly supports small businesses, but argued that "you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business".

The dispute took another turn after podcast host Pablo Torre obtained and released CCTV footage from inside the store, depicting Clarkson wearing a yellow shirt and a baseball cap.

The footage, which contains no audio, appears to show Clarkson browsing items, pointing towards Molly and speaking with staff.

After the exchange, Clarkson appears to put items she was carrying back on a shelf before leaving.

According to Torre, Clarkson spent less than five minutes inside the store.

Because the footage has no sound, it does not resolve the central disagreement over what was said.

'Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger'

As the dispute spread online, Art of Play said it was overwhelmed by the reaction.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store," it said in an earlier statement.

The store later said it hoped it could "clear things up" with Clarkson.

Store co-owner Adam Rubin has since accused Clarkson of directing unwanted attention towards the business.

"We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers," Rubin told reporters outside the store.

"Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger."

Rubin described the backlash as "asymmetrical social warfare" and later told radio station 1010 WINS there had clearly been a "miscommunication".

He said the attention had become overwhelming and that staff had turned off the store's phones.

The concerns escalated this week when a man filmed himself outside the store yelling expletives and accusing staff of "racially profiling" Clarkson.

"We feel no ill will against Kelly Clarkson," Rubin said. "We invite her to come back and enjoy the store."

Where is Molly now?

Molly is still hanging on the store's wall, seeing much more foot traffic than usual, and sporting a much higher price tag.

Following the dispute, Art of Play replaced the original $15,000 sign with a new price tag, listing Molly for US$15 million ($21.4 million).

Art of Play's store owners said they told Clarkson that Molly, pictured being installed by its creator Bliss Kolb, was permanently attached to the wall and was not for sale. Source: Supplied / Art of Play / 69Atlantic

The sign describes Molly as the "world's most famous singing bird automata".

Whether anyone buys her remains to be seen.

title: Shoebridge pressed on what Greens knew after Steele-John investigation ordered

In brief A Greens senator has stepped aside as allegations trigger a probe.

An independent process will examine a letter containing allegations related to comments about women.

Greens leader David Shoebridge has refused to say whether the party will release the findings of an inquiry into allegations against Greens senator Jordon Steele-John.

Steele-John,32, has rejected allegations that he made inappropriate comments towards women and has taken leave from the Greens party room.

Shoebridge denies he knew about historic complaints about the Western Australian senator between 2017 and 2025, until a letter from seven Greens members demanding an investigation into "concerning behaviour" landed on his desk this week.

"I've been leader now for two weeks, and when I received these complaints, I took the most timely action that I believe you could take, and I'd ask people to judge me and on the response that’s been taken, the timely response that's been taken," Shoebridge told reporters on Friday.

"This is a process that will be commissioned by the WA Greens, and the parameters that we are very clear about is it will be fair, and it will be independent, and it will be timely. But it is not my role to put parameters around what we have said must be and will be an independent process.

"And we are committed to undertaking that process, and committed to doing justice to the matters that have been raised, and justice to any party that has been involved in the matter, and I think that should be actually a bedrock. That should actually be a bedrock of politics."

The letter sent to Shoebridge contains accusations he says the party takes "incredibly seriously".

"When matters like this are raised, they require a fair and independent and timely process for them to be dealt with. The WA Greens are commissioning that process," he said.

The senator will self-refer matters outlined in the letter to an independent complaints process.

title: 'Inconsequential': Trump's new press secretary confirms she didn't pass the bar exam
text:
In brief Donald Trump's new White House press secretary has said the results of her bar exam were "somewhat inconsequential".

She said she moved to China shortly after graduating and "knew I wouldn't need the bar in China".

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia appeared to confirm on Friday that she did not pass a United States bar exam, following mounting questions over her legal credentials days into her new role.

Zacharia had repeatedly presented herself as a lawyer during media appearances, and US President Donald Trump described her as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment last week.

However, journalists found no record of her being licensed to practice law in any US state, spurring questions about how she had represented herself.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Zacharia sat the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011 but did not pass.

Obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practice law. California's state bar confirmed to US media that it had no record of Zacharia holding a license under either her married or maiden name.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Appearing on the right-wing Real America's Voice network on Friday, Zacharia said she had been in a long-distance relationship during law school and moved after graduating to be with her husband, who worked at an American private equity company in China.

The 41-year-old said she had pre-registered to take the bar but was "distracted and overwhelmed and excited" to be married.

"The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China and we left shortly thereafter," she said, without explicitly stating if she had passed or failed.

"After moving to China, I think I didn't really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on, and I was offered a job at an international practice division of a Chinese law firm."

"There's no Chinese bar. I had enough credentials — which was my law degree — to be able to do this practice."

Foreign nationals cannot sit China's bar exam. However, they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.

Zacharia acknowledged there was controversy over her decision to present herself as a "lawyer" but branded it "misinformation" and "miscommunication".

She said she had consulted "many people" in the legal field and determined she could call herself a lawyer, but not an "attorney at law" or "Katie Zacharia, Esquire". She said she'd been advised she could provide legal analysis but not advice.

"It’s unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp," she said on Real America's Voice.

"The truth is ... I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."

According to a CNN investigation, Zacharia shared at least 15 social media posts, such as those from Fox News and other news segments, identifying her as an "attorney" over the past two years.

A tumultuous first week

Zacharia, a devotee of Trump's right-wing MAGA movement, was not well known to the public before she was elevated to the country's most prominent podium.

Her first briefing, which lasted just 15 minutes, featured praise of Trump and a stumble in which she accidentally referred to the president instead of her husband.

She took just three questions, all from organisations considered to cover Trump favourably: Fox News, the right-wing website Breitbart and the Daily Mail.

Zacharia previously served as an adviser to Trump Media and Technology, the group behind the president's Truth Social platform, and as a legal adviser to conservative group Fix California, according to a LinkedIn profile.

Katie Zacharia seemed to suggest she passed a bar exam in China earlier in the week, sparking further confusion. Source: Getty / Win McNamee

Before taking on the White House role, she frequently appeared on conservative media outlets Fox News and Newsmax.

In response to initial questions and reports about Zacharia's legal background, the White House said Zacharia "moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law".

Within days, a US watchdog group had filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a license.

Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

title: It's a risk in some of Australia's favourite destinations. Now there's a vaccine
text: In brief Heading to Bali or another tourism hotspot? A new vaccine may change how you prepare for your trip. Here's what to know about dengue fever, where the risk of contracting it is highest, and how it can be mitigated. Some of the most popular travel destinations for Australians are also places where dengue is common. Prevention has traditionally relied on avoiding mosquito bites. But with the dengue vaccine Qdenga now available in Australia, travellers have another way to protect themselves. Deciding whether to get vaccinated isn't always straightforward. Here's what you need to know. What is dengue? Dengue is a viral illness spread by mosquitoes. It typically causes fever, headache, body aches, nausea and rash. There is no specific treatment. Most people get better in one to two weeks, but for some, fatigue can persist for weeks or months. Some people will develop severe illness and need hospital care and, in some cases, dengue is fatal. There are four types of dengue virus. Infection with any type can make you sick. After infection, you're protected against that type in the future, but can still be infected by the other three. A second infection with a different type can sometimes cause more severe illness than the first. The reasons are complex, but one is that antibodies left over from the first infection can make it easier for the new virus to infect cells. People who live in, or frequently travel to, places where dengue is common are more likely to be exposed to different dengue virus types over time. Where is the risk highest? Although mosquitoes that can spread dengue are found in tropical parts of central and far north Queensland, local dengue outbreaks are now rare thanks to a successful public health program involving the release of mosquitoes infected with a bacterium that blocks the spread of viruses. For Australians, the main risk is during overseas travel. More than 1,900 dengue cases were reported in Australia in 2025, largely in returned travellers. Between 2012 and 2022, Indonesia, Thailand and India were the most common places Australian travellers got dengue. Some popular destinations for Australians, such as Bali, have frequent outbreaks. Dengue can be more common at certain times of year, and outbreaks can cause case numbers to rise sharply from one year to the next. The risk in many regions is also increasing as a changing climate creates more favourable conditions for the mosquitoes that spread it. Why has developing a dengue vaccine been so difficult? A dengue vaccine needs to protect against all four virus types and not increase the risk of severe disease if someone gets infected with dengue after they have been vaccinated. An earlier vaccine, Dengvaxia, was found to increase the risk of severe dengue in some children who had never had dengue before, and then got dengue after being vaccinated. That experience means new dengue vaccines have been closely studied and assessed for safety. How well does Qdenga work, and is it safe? Qdenga uses weakened dengue viruses to teach the immune system to protect against all four types of dengue virus. It is given as two doses, three months apart. Millions of doses have now been given worldwide, and an increased risk of severe dengue has not been seen following vaccination. In a large study of children and teenagers living in countries where dengue is common, the vaccine prevented about 80 per cent of illness and more than 95 per cent of hospitalisations in the first year. Protection against hospitalisation remained high for more than four years. READ MORE The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers Like all vaccines, Qdenga can cause side effects. In recent European studies, around half of travellers receiving Qdenga reported side effects, most commonly pain or redness where the injection was given, headache, fatigue or muscle aches. Most were mild and lasted one to three days. There are still some gaps in the evidence. Most studies looking at how well Qdenga prevents dengue have involved children and teenagers. Studies in adults have focused more on immune responses and safety than on directly measuring protection against dengue. Among people who have never had dengue, Qdenga provides strong protection against types one and two, but there's more uncertainty around protection against types three and four. As a result, different countries have made different recommendations about who should receive Qdenga. Qdenga also isn't suitable for everyone. Because it is a live vaccine, people with weakened immune systems cannot have it, and it's not recommended during pregnancy. So, should I get vaccinated? Getting vaccinated isn't a simple yes-or-no decision. Advice may differ depending on where you are going, whether you have had dengue before and how much exposure you are likely to have in the future. A discussion with a health professional can help you decide whether vaccination is right for you. In Australia, Qdenga is recommended for travellers aged four or older who have had dengue before, and for those who haven't but expect to spend a long time, or make repeated trips, to places where dengue occurs. It costs around AUD$300 for two doses. For someone who hasn't had dengue and is only taking a shorter trip, the decision is more individual. Factors such as where you're going, how long you'll be there and whether there is a current outbreak can all influence whether vaccination is worthwhile. What else can I do to avoid dengue? Whether or not you get vaccinated, avoiding mosquito bites remains important. Aedes aegypti, the main mosquito that spreads dengue, tends to bite during the day, often around the lower legs. Travellers should use insect repellent outdoors during the day. It's a good idea to buy it before you leave, as products available overseas may not be tested to Australian standards. Wearing loose-fitting long pants and covered shoes can provide extra protection. Bed nets can also help if you're sleeping during the day, particularly somewhere without insect screens. title: The growing issue that could make migrating to Australia less attractive
text:
IN BRIEF: Australia's unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent.

An expert says if it rises people may be deterred from coming to Australia.

Australia needs a strong labour market to attract skilled migrants, an expert says, as the unemployment rate hovers above expectations and is expected to rise.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.

The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.

It's expected to rise over the next two years, as the government and Opposition have all sought to reduce net overseas migration (NOM).

The International Monetary Fund forecast unemployment in Australia would climb by 0.3 per cent, from 4.4 per cent on average this year to 4.7 per cent next year, at which point the number of Australians out of work would approach 800,000.

Economics and public policy commentator Abul Rizvi told SBS News a weak labour market would turn away not only migrants, but also Australian citizens.

"What you will see is an increase in departures and reduction in arrivals," he told SBS News.

But Rizvi said the unemployment rate in Australia would have to rise "much more significantly" for there to be the kind of "exodus" that was seen in previous years, including during the 1990-1991 recession.

Coalition migration approach 'illogical'

Rizvi has questioned the federal Coalition’s migration target, saying it doesn't take into account labour market factors.

The Coalition's migration plan, released last week, vowed to get NOM down to 100,000 — slashing temporary migrant visas, student visas and bridging visas, while increasing the number of skilled visas by 100,000.

Speaking on ABC's Insiders program on Sunday, Opposition leader Angus Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.

"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.

"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.

READ MORE The surprising health condition some people develop after moving to Australia

Rizvi said the Coalition's plan was "illogical" and avoided discussing the state of Australia's labour market.

"The Coalition wants to do two contradictory things at the same time," he said.

"They want to reduce the level of NOM, which requires a much weaker labour market. At the same time, they want to increase the level of skilled migration, which requires a strong labour market.

Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.

One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which it says will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy.

They generally arrive in the country after finishing their education, while the average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Motivations for coming to Australia

As debate continues over migration policy, analysis from libertarian think tank, the Centre for Independent Studies released this week, found that economic and job opportunities were the top reason first generation migrants self-reported for coming to Australia, and that their motivations differed greatly from what Australian-born citizens expected.

The next most common reason the report found was cultural factors, such as the Australian lifestyle, values and customs, while Australian-born citizens were much less likely to assume this as a motivation for migration.

The data on 3,552 voters across Australia found that new Australians were far less likely than Australian-born citizens to say that access to a strong social safety net or welfare was important to migrants’ decision to come.

It was a similar picture for the Australian environment, with 31 per cent of new Australians saying factors such as the weather and cleanliness were a reason for migrating, compared with what 11 per cent of Australian-born respondents thought.

Skill mismatch

Successive studies have found that even during times of economic strength, it was difficult for migrants, and especially refugees, to find appropriate work in Australia.

Research from public policy think tank the Committee for Economic Development of Australia, found nearly a quarter of permanent skilled migrants in Australia were working in a job beneath their skill level, or experiencing a "skill mismatch", which was at a substantially higher level among migrants on Family and Humanitarian visas.

It also found that, on average, recent migrants earned significantly less than the Australian-born population, across all temporary and permanent visa types.

In the Scanlan Foundation's 2026 Multiculturalism in Focus report, published in February, nearly half of interviewees reported that securing meaningful employment was their greatest challenge after arriving in Australia.

Common barriers included non-recognition of overseas qualifications and the disadvantage of lacking local work experience.

Migration’s boost for local workers

Migration has been found to reduce unemployment for domestic workers in international studies, including a 2025 study on OECD countries that found a "significant" negative relationship between net migration rate and the unemployment rate of Australian-born workers.

The report found that Australia demonstrated well-planned immigration approaches through active selection methods, accepting professionals with high qualifications while providing integration assistance to new residents.

Australia’s economy could absorb increasing numbers of migrants while still providing employment opportunities for both Australian-born workers and immigrants.

A series of OECD reports published from 2023 to 2024 also found that Australians of all ages and genders benefited from migration, which boosted the labour productivity and employment of Australian‑born workers.

title: Revealed: State's $80 billion compensation headache in a fuel crisis
text:
IN BRIEF Victoria considered overhauling decades-old fuel emergency laws amid fears of substantial legal liability.

Proposed changes were never introduced, leaving any overhaul to the next parliament.

Victorian taxpayers could be on the hook for tens of billions of dollars in the event of a major fuel crisis under legislation that allows payment for those suffering economic loss.

The prospect of a budget black hole of up to $80 billion had forced the state government to consider updating its 1970s-era fuel emergency laws, which allow the preservation and allocation of fuel supplies during declared fuel emergencies.

The rethink came in June amid higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East and as the federal government extended fuel excise relief.

But the legislative amendments were ultimately not introduced before the end of the parliamentary sitting year, meaning any changes would now have to wait until the next parliament, with the state election due in late November.

Federal, state and territory governments can declare fuel emergencies, with the Victorian government initially appearing concerned over what liability it could be exposed to in the event it used powers under its laws.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Such declarations are made if any kind of fuel is likely to become unavailable, allowing compensation to be paid to those who suffer financial losses as a result of being forced to comply with ministerial directions.

The broad powers allow the minister to control, direct, restrict or prohibit the production, supply, distribution, sale, use or consumption of the fuel; or direct at what times and places services may be used.

The laws also allow people to be compensated for complying with the directions if they suffer losses or damages.

"Any sums required to be paid or provided for the purposes of this Act shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund," the law states, referring to the state's primary financial account into which all revenue is paid.

Declaring a state of emergency under the Fuel Emergency Act is rare. A 2020 parliamentary library research paper found the most recent declaration was in 2004, after a factory fire triggered a briquette shortage. The state government invoked the powers and secured the remaining briquette supply to keep hospital boilers running.

At the time, and still today, there was no indication of any immediate threat to Australia's or the state's liquid fuel supply.

Prices, however, have risen across the country following the end of temporary fuel excise relief, and against the backdrop of continued conflict in the Middle East and volatility in global oil markets.

The war has also sparked questions over Australia's energy security and how the nation might be impacted if there were severe disruptions or shortages.

In the case of Victoria, if it were to expose itself to compensation claims through the use of emergency powers, the state government could face a legal burden of up to $80 billion that would ultimately fall to taxpayers, according to a June draft government proposal seen by SBS News.

The potentially heavy cost was a key driver for the changes, the proposal states, as well as the inordinate amount of time and money it would take to manage claims and potential lawsuits.

The state government believed the current laws were out of step with other jurisdictions, where some fuel emergency regimes provide explicit immunity from certain legal claims, while compensation may be unavailable or subject to tighter thresholds.

A Victorian government spokesperson had previously told SBS News the Fuel Emergency Act would be updated to align it with other states and territories, ensuring a "consistent, modern approach" to managing fuel supply disruptions.

Asked last week why the government had not gone ahead with the amendments and whether it still believed the laws would expose it to substantial financial liability in the event of a state-declared fuel emergency, a spokesperson did not answer directly.

"The review of Victoria's Fuel Emergency Act was part of national contingency planning in response to global fuel supply risks," the spokesperson said.

"Victoria is now better prepared to respond to any fuel emergency, with stronger national coordination, better visibility of fuel supplies and clear arrangements to manage disruptions."

The spokesperson said the state's fuel supply "remains strong" and that the government was working with the federal government and industry to "prepare for any potential disruption".

The spokesperson did not address how the potential liability of up to $80 billion was calculated.

Earlier this year, Australia was gripped by concerns over fuel supply sparked by global oil shortages due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply flows.

The head of the International Energy Agency warned the global economy was facing a "major threat" to supply, describing the situation as worse than the two oil crises of the 1970s combined, as well as the crisis caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Political figures such as One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce had called for federal fuel rationing measures in the cities to mitigate the impact of shortages in the regions, calling on the federal government to enact a state of emergency over the situation.

The federal government had reportedly crisis-planned in the event of a national shortage, with measures including fuel rationing and limits on fuel purchase per vehicle, according to a report by Guardian Australia in May.

title: 'Completely reversed': Why more Australian households are feeling miserable
text:
In Brief Inflation, high interest rates and rising unemployment are keeping pressure on households.

Economic misery is expected to remain above historical averages until at least 2028.

Australians are feeling increasingly miserable about the economy, with financial pressures unlikely to ease anytime soon, according to new analysis.

New research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) found economic "misery" has returned to post-pandemic highs, wiping out improvements made since 2023 and leaving the country on track for several more years of elevated financial strain.

The think tank expects misery levels to remain well above recent historical averages through to at least the end of 2028, as households continue to grapple with inflation, high interest rates and a gradually weakening labour market.

Fresh data released on Thursday added to those concerns, showing Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

CEDA's misery index combines inflation, unemployment and interest rates to provide a broad measure of the economic pressures facing households.

"When those things go up, there's more of a financial pinch for households and there's a little bit more pressure on the pocketbook," CEDA head of economics Liam Dillon told SBS News.

Progress 'completely reversed'

CEDA says higher prices and borrowing costs have been the main contributors to the recent rise in economic misery.

"What we found is that since 2023, the misery index had been coming down as inflation was trending lower and the Reserve Bank was able to lower interest rates accordingly," Dillon said.

"Since then though, inflation's been a little bit more persistent than we had hoped. That's led the Reserve Bank to increase interest rates to 15-year highs."

"The combination of those things means that the progress on lowering that economic misery has now been completely reversed and we're back at 2023 levels."

Steadily rising unemployment, high inflation and rate hikes have led to a three-year high of "misery" levels in Australia. Source: SBS News

After briefly returning to the Reserve Bank's two to three per cent target range in 2025, annual inflation rose to four per cent over the year to August.

The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates four times this year, taking the official cash rate to its highest level in 15 years, with some economists expecting another increase before the end of 2026.

The report also points to broader signs of economic pessimism, with consumer confidence remaining at levels comparable to those seen during the pandemic.

Unemployment exceeding forecasts

While inflation and interest rates have driven the latest increase in the misery index, the labour market has helped cushion the impact on many households.

But that source of support is beginning to weaken.

In the decade before the pandemic, unemployment was the largest contributor to Australia's economic misery, averaging 5.5 per cent of the population and peaking at 6.3 per cent in late 2014.

Since the pandemic, unemployment has remained comparatively low, averaging around four per cent.

But fresh figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday suggest labour market conditions are continuing to soften.

Australia's unemployment rate has risen above market expectations to 4.7 per cent in September. Source: SBS News

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.

The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.

Employment fell by 39,300 people over the month, while the number of unemployed Australians increased by 8,900.

The result also exceeded the Reserve Bank's forecast for unemployment to reach 4.5 per cent by the December quarter.

Despite the deterioration, Dillon said the jobs market remained a relative source of strength for the economy.

"What we've seen is that even though unemployment has been rising, the labour market is still showing signs of resilience and that's really helping to support households," he said.

About 177,000 jobs have been added since the start of the year, according to CEDA.

Dillon said that had helped insulate households from some of the effects of higher inflation and interest rates, while household savings remain above the decade average in the years before the pandemic.

The remedy to misery

The report argues reducing economic misery remains difficult because efforts to bring down inflation can often come at the expense of employment and economic activity.

To return inflation to the Reserve Bank's target range, it has largely relied on higher interest rates, increasing pressure on households already facing elevated living costs.

Minutes from the Reserve Bank's September meeting, released this week, showed staff were increasingly concerned weak productivity growth may mean unemployment needs to be higher than previously thought to keep inflation stable.

Dillon said stronger productivity growth offered the best long-term solution because it could ease pressure across all three parts of the misery index.

READ MORE The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality

"What we suggest and what we argue through this is that really the only way to get at all three drivers of misery is to boost productivity growth," he said.

"That's a challenge and a long-term one at that, but really this index shows why that's so important."

CEDA expects misery levels to remain above recent historical averages through to the end of 2028 based on current trends.

title: House prices are falling. So why are first-home buyers disappearing?
text:
In brief A key group is abandoning the housing market in growing numbers.

New figures have shown affordability pressures are still biting.

Australians trying to buy their first home are being driven away by strict serviceability testing and higher interest rates, with mortgage demand in its sharpest fall since 2022.

Overall mortgage demand dropped 19.2 per cent year-on-year in September, despite house prices across the country slipping 1.1 per cent, according to data from credit reporting body Equifax.

This was coupled with a fall in new home loan applications, which dropped 22.1 per cent compared to 12 months ago.

Australian households were taking a decisive step back, Equifax chief solutions officer Kevin James said.

"This is the largest year-on-year decline in first home buyer mortgage demand since December 2022, and baseline prices for properties remain high despite recent market dips," he told The Australian Associated Press news agency.
