Younger people were the hardest hit, as mortgages for 18 to 25-year-olds fell by a quarter, and those for 26 to 35-year-olds slumped 22.5 per cent in September.

Aspiring first home buyers continue to struggle in the property market, with several compounding factors such as strict serviceability testing, high interest rates, and spiralling living costs making it difficult for young Australians to achieve the dream of home ownership.

James said that unfortunately, there was no quick fix.

"There is no silver bullet solution; each element needs to be considered when looking for ways to make the market more accessible for this cohort," James said.

Even though property values had been easing, baseline prices were still high — with average first home buyer mortgage sizes hovering at record levels of $743,000.

James said many potential first home buyers were finding it hard to raise a deposit and afford mortgage repayments without institutional or family support.

Fewer people were moving to new lenders, with lender-switching falling 8.8 per cent compared to a year earlier, after a nearly flat performance in August.

"In the current economic climate, strict regulatory serviceability assessments appear to be holding borrowers in place," James said.

"Many existing mortgage holders wanting to shop around for a better rate are likely finding themselves unable to clear the serviceability needed, effectively locking them into their current arrangements."

Meanwhile, Australians aged 56 and over helped drive a surge in credit cards.

Credit card demand rose by a tenth compared to a year earlier, driven by a 36.3 per cent spike among borrowers aged 56 and above.

It's a different story for young people, as 18–35-year-olds pull back across the credit spectrum.

title: For years, it led nowhere. Now North Korea is opening it
text:
In brief A new bridge between North Korea and China has been opened, 12 years after it was completed.

The move is expected to strengthen trade between the two countries.

A new bridge linking China and North Korea opened on Thursday after more than a decade of delay in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries.

The four-lane, 3km New Yalu River Bridge will connect the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju.

Trucks bearing the North Korean and Chinese flags began passing in both directions over the bridge in the late morning, reporters for the Agence France-Presse news agency at the scene said.

The bridge was first expected to open in 2014 after China apparently completed construction of access roads, customs facilities and other related infrastructure on its side. But the date passed with no sign of an opening and without North Korea doing corresponding works on its side.

At that time, it prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city.

A lack of substantial work on the North Korean side prompted speculation that North Korea was wary of an increase in economic dependence or was unhappy with China voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program. Some observers said North Korea and China also differed over the location of the bridge.

Bridge expected to bolster trade links

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Wednesday the new bridge will further promote economic, trade and "people-to-people exchanges".

"China and the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] are friendly neighbours linked by rivers and mountains," Mao Ning said. She added the bridge is an important "project for connectivity" between the two countries.

The new link is expected to lessen the burden on an existing yet aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70 per cent of official trade between the two countries. The old bridge built in 1937 carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time.

The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border, which stretches more than 1,400km.

The new bridge's opening will likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually. But in the short term, trade won't likely result in a sharp increase in Chinese exports to North Korea as Beijing would take Pyongyang's interests into consideration to some extent, according to a recent report by Gyubeom Kim, an expert at Seoul's state-run Institute for National Security Strategy.

North Korea's export of processed goods, food products, cosmetics and alcoholic beverages to China could increase, Kim said.

Relations with Russia and China

The bridge's opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a 1km road bridge over the Tumen River as part of their efforts to cement relations.

Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about the opening of the North Korea-Russia bridge, which the Russian government said would allow daily passage of up to 300 vehicles through a newly built border crossing point.

The North Korea-China bridge is much bigger and likely capable of carrying round-the-clock, two-way traffic including containers and heavy cargo trucks, according to Jeong Eun-i, an analyst from South Korea's Institute for National Unification.

China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.

Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve the economy and build a front against the United States. China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98 per cent of North Korea's external trade was with China.

The bridge's opening has been anticipated since Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing's willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

title: The $2.9 trillion corner of Australia's economy at the centre of a tax war
text:
Key Points Small business groups warn 350,000 family firms face higher taxes or costly restructures.

Coalition vows to repeal changes as compliance costs top $1 billion.

A multi-billion-dollar gap and a reignited political divide has opened up between small businesses and the government over a new policy taxing trillion-dollar trust schemes.

The government plans to close a tax advantage many workers can't access by imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax on the net income of 840,000 trusts that allow wealthy investors and family businesses to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings. Australian trusts have combined assets of $2.9 trillion with annual income of $600 billion.

The changes are projected to raise $4.47 billion in 2029/30 after they begin on 1 July 2028. Treasury data shows trusts are overwhelmingly used by Australia's top 10 per cent of income earners who receive about two-thirds of distributions, while the bottom 10 per cent receive one per cent.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the reforms affect fewer than 10 per cent of small businesses.

"Small businesses and others using discretionary trusts can access rollover relief from 1 July 2027 if they want to restructure, or can make an election for tax purposes to be exempt from the minimum tax, for as long as they continue to make distributions to pre-nominated beneficiaries in line with an upfront nomination," Chalmers said on Wednesday.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute, David Richardson, told SBS News the changes plug a tax-dodging loophole used by wealthy people to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings.

"The ambiguity of who owns what in the trust means they become a vehicle for putting assets away, where it's very hard for bankruptcy proceedings to access them," Richardson said. "It's hard for the Family Court to know what's going on. So, generally, family trusts, even when they're taxed at 30 per cent, will still be useful for somebody on very high incomes, where the marginal tax rate is 47 cents."

That small businesses, and others are unhappy with the change, "shows you that they're presently doing well out of a trust structure", he said.

"They wouldn't be complaining unless they were genuinely avoiding what they would have to pay as either an individual sole trader or as the principal of some sort of corporate structure."

Australian Council of Social Service CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie said the reforms restore some "basic economic fairness".

"It is not fair that someone earning $200,000 or more, who would usually pay 47 per cent tax on extra income, can bring that rate down to 30 per cent or less by passing income through a discretionary trust to their adult children or a private company, while an average worker pays tax at a rate of 30 per cent of the next dollar earned," Goldie said.

Why are small businesses unhappy?

The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia CEO Skye Cappuccio said after months of consultation "fundamental problems" remain, forcing 350,000 family and small businesses structured this way to choose between "a substantial tax increase", or restructuring costs in the thousands of dollars for professional fees, duties and administration.

Credit: Australia Institute

"These are not genuine choices. They are bad options that will make operating a small family business harder and more expensive," Cappuccio said.

"These are small family businesses that have legitimately used trusts for decades to protect assets, manage succession and plan for the future," Cappuccio said.

"This policy targets a business structure rather than the conduct the government is concerned about. There are more targeted ways to address tax integrity without imposing unnecessary costs on genuine small businesses.

"Queensland and Western Australian enterprises will be hit hardest by the changes because stamp duty may apply if a business there restructures its assets."

What's the political divide and controversy?

The Coalition failed to stall the laws on Wednesday, but opposition leader Angus Taylor said the Coalition will go to the election with a "policy of axing the tax".

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said, "small and family businesses face a bill of up to $13.3 billion for the cost of valuations, advisers and stamp duty because our taxaholic treasurer broke his election promise and can’t kick his spending addiction".

"The treasurer has rewritten this tax again and again since budget night because he doesn’t understand his own policy or the damage it does. Every backdown is an admission it should never have been proposed in the first place," Wilson said.

Trusts excluded from the changes include deceased estates, disability, superannuation, charities, farms and fixed trusts.

READ MORE How the ATO found itself embroiled in a battle over credit cards that forced a rethink

The Housing Industry Association warned this is a new tax on tradies, and builders that diverts their attention from building the homes Australia desperately needs."

Greens leader David Shoebridge said on Wednesday there are too many concessions being made and will refer the bill to a Senate inquiry and that claims about restructuring costs should be supported by detailed modelling.

"We want to make sure that we don't, in passing this legislation, create that additional loophole," Shoebridge said. "This is about ensuring that there's a fair level playing field across business, but also across society, and that's our focus.

"If the Coalition is going to put a figure out like that ($13 billion), they need to back it up with numbers (and modelling)."

Will this really cost businesses $13 billion?

Treasury estimates the cost to businesses will be $141.5 million annually plus $940 million during an implementation phase.

But the Coalition and Wilson say the cost will be up to $13.3 billion based on a Wilson Asset Management estimate.

Wilson ran a successful campaign against changes to franking credits by coordinating with Wilson Asset Management in 2019.

But CPA Australia tax lead Jenny Wong told SBS News the Coalition’s figure includes stamp duty, and Treasury’s doesn’t. But there is no source or method listed as to how they arrived at their number.

"Our estimate is $2 billion to $2.8 billion, for advice alone (and) covers the cost of working out what to do across roughly 850,000 trusts, before anyone restructures or elects (beneficiaries)," Wong said. "The bill leaves 12 rules to be made later by the minister, up from 10, and ATO [Australian Taxation Office] guidance won’t come until after the law passes."

The government has given families a way to avoid restructuring, and "that deserves credit", she said.

"But for those who still have to restructure, nothing in this bill makes it cheaper. Stamp duty can be most of the bill, and the Commonwealth can’t waive it,” Wong said.

"We support dealing with inappropriate income splitting (done) simply, fairly and in proportion," Wong said. "On that test, there is still work to do."

Treasury's analysis estimates that restructuring a family business can cost between $9,536 and $23,436 and that restructuring could cost family businesses more than the tax itself.

title: Russian facilities were attacked. Then came a viral theory
text:
Key Points Ukraine has launched strikes on three data centres used by Russian technology platform Yandex over the last week.

Several posts claiming a resulting decrease in Russian bot activity have been widely circulated.

A series of Ukrainian strikes on data centres in Russia had Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claiming an additional win.

"When our strikes reached Yandex’s data centres, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms," he told participants at the Warsaw Security Forum this week.

"There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations. Because there were fewer bots."

Russia had previously targeted Ukrainian data centres and telecommunication infrastructure.

But as the latest round of strikes had users celebrating a drop in Russian misinformation, experts say the reality is more complicated.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

A change in web traffic

In the past week, Ukraine has struck three of the five main data centres used by Russian technology company Yandex, often considered Russia's version of Google.

A widely shared graph of data from US tech firm Cloudflare showed a sharp drop-off for bot traffic shortly after one of the strikes.

A Polish political scientist shared a post linking the strikes to a sharp drop in activity supportive of Germany's far-right AfD party. He later deleted the X post after finding the graph was AI-generated, but it had already circulated widely. A similar graphic was also shared by a Czech member of the European Parliament on X.

The Ukrainian strikes damaged Yandex infrastructure, with a Kremlin spokesperson saying the provider was "currently facing difficulties".

Yandex is used for search, email, file storage, food delivery, ride-sharing, and more in Russia. Source: AAP / Kirill Kukhmar

Olivia Shen is the director of strategic technologies at the United States Studies Centre. She says while a drop in bot traffic from Yandex has been observed, there has been no definitive evidence that it resulted in an impact on dis- or misinformation.

"A company like Yandex has bots crawl on the internet all the time, but they do really basic things like indexing web pages and optimising its search engines, just as you would expect Google to do," she said.

"So, it's not really surprising that when the Yandex data centres are taken out of action, there's fewer Yandex bots sending out automated requests to websites.

"Not all bots are equal, and they don't all do the same thing."

What are bots?

The term bot is used to describe any automated process completed online. It's also, however, often used to describe the actions of malicious actors.

Dr Kateryna Kasianenko studies how online searching practices relate to real-world crises. She said Cloudflare uses a broad definition of bots.

"There is a chance that what we call social media bots on Russia's side would have been impacted by [the strikes]. But the extent of that is quite hard to evaluate at this stage," she said.

"It's been really interesting to see the attempts to actually evaluate whether or not there was indeed a drop in engagement or also the spread of problematic narratives on Russia's behalf and actors that Russia may support, like AfD, Donald Trump and others.

"The evidence so far is quite mixed."

Kasianenko says it has brought more attention to "the mechanics behind Russia's efforts to control [the] information space".

She says it's quite hard for a regular user to accurately identify whether something online was created by a person or a bot, especially when the interaction involves amplification, such as liking and reposting content.

"Russia does deploy a mixed approach where they have these very handcrafted, deliberate human messages, and they also use automation for things like amplification, retweeting and likes," she said.

"It's very hard to know whether those types of engagements were generated by a human or an automated account."

Shen says this is further complicated by a tendency to label difficult viewpoints as bots, rather than grappling with the complexity of differing beliefs held within Russia.

"I don't think just dismissing those views, those legitimately held views as mis- or disinformation, or as the behaviour of bots, is helpful in bridging those gaps between Russians and Ukrainians or Russians and the rest of the world," she said.

A perceived decline in pro-Russian views online could be explained by Russian citizens not being able to access the internet, instead of damage to bot networks.

Dr Olga Boichak, a senior lecturer in digital cultures at the University of Sydney, researches the weaponisation of digital technologies. She says we need more research to empirically prove whether a sizeable reduction in the amount of troll and bot messaging has occurred. Shen said this situation is "a perfect opportunity for a natural experiment to actually collect the data on that".

The physical dimension of misinformation

Boichak said these strikes have exposed a critical vulnerability: "physical infrastructure matters".

Mis- and disinformation are normally treated as activities happening online, but she said the breadth of potential forms it can take makes it difficult to contain.

"Not all of them involve spreading falsehoods. Sometimes it would be manufacturing a few competing versions of truth. Sometimes it would be circulating different rumours. Sometimes it will be circulating memes. Sometimes it would be bullying and harassment of the people who are activists or working in some space," she said.

"Our traditional containment methods sometimes fall short because they don't recognise something as an influence operation.

"I think that is a big lesson here that democracies need to consider various other ways, ways that are deeper in the infrastructural levels to contain these attempts and disinformation."

Data centres are becoming an increasingly acceptable military target, according to Shen.

"I think that's a bit concerning because this is digital infrastructure that takes down the internet for a lot of ordinary users, not just military operatives or people deliberately spreading influence campaigns," she said.

Boichak says Russia's regime of "digital authoritarianism" makes damage to physical infrastructure more severe, with much of the country reliant on Yandex, as a result of the ongoing blocking of Western platforms.

The most unexpected trend of the season is the cummerbund, with wrapped waists appearing at Celine, Valentino and Ralph Lauren alongside a host of indie brands such as Kallmeyer, Conner Ives and Mithridate. Here, the cummerbund sheds its stuffy, swashbuckling associations with rented formal tuxedos and ’80s pastel suits for a modern, genderless look. Stylist Jade Fox wears a vintage Gucci blouse and Harris Tapper trousers with a foam green lace offcut fashioned into a cummerbund. Sam Mooy The fashion item can be seen snatching in the waist of a slouchy sweater, adding structure to a slinky slip dress or adding heft to billowing pants. There are pleated cummerbunds, intricately beaded cummerbunds and jacquard cummerbunds – take your pick. As with most trends, this isn’t the cummerbund’s first go-around in fashion.

Advertisement

They made frequent appearances in the work of Yves Saint Laurent – accessorising a Le Smoking suit or adding definition to a brocade, drop-waist dress in the 1977 “Les Chinoises” collection. Jean Paul Gaultier, Helmut Lang and Anthony Vaccarello, among many others, all interpreted the accessory in their own ways. The name itself is an anglicisation of kamarband, an Urdu word (derived from Persian) meaning waistband. Typically woven from cotton, silk or wool, its distinctive pleats served more than just an aesthetic purpose, but could handily hold tobacco pouches, currency or ceremonial daggers. A Rajput Warrior, c. 1650, wearing a kamarband. Getty Images

Advertisement

London-based researcher, archivist and founder of South Asia Archive Sanam Sindhi, says locating the style in one specific time and place is difficult. “It’s an accoutrement that has long been in existence and exchange across many cultures in South, South West and Central Asia, each region with their own way of fashioning it,” she says. In colonial India, the cummerbund became a staple in British military officer uniforms, earning the name “cholera belt” as the thick fabric provided warmth and protection against the region’s harsh climate. “Though the British were eager to maintain strict sartorial boundaries between themselves and Indians during their occupation, the kamarband was one of the few items they did adopt into their own wardrobes due to its incredible practicality,” Sindhi explains.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Trends The $100 million fashion moment 65,000 years in the making “Taking it back with them to Britain in the 1800s, it eventually became the ‘cummerbund’, misappropriated as a signature of black-tie dressing.” Jade Fox, a Sydney-based stylist and writer behind Substack Consider This, was inspired after seeing the style pop up at fashion month. “The menswear Celine show was stunning. It was about blurring the lines between evening wear and casual wear,” she says. “We went through this phase of seeing a lot of oversized items with not much shape. And with the cummerbund, the waist is back.”

Advertisement

“It’s adding texture, volume and changing the proportion of something just by adding something to the waist,” says Jade Fox of the cummerbund. Sam Mooy Fox realised she had everything she needed to fashion her own cummerbund by raiding her arsenal of vintage silk scarves. “I haven’t actually bought anything new, and that’s one of the things that I love about the trend,” she says. “It’s adding texture, volume and changing the proportion of something just by adding something to the waist.”

Advertisement

Fabric remnants are another easy entry point. “I was wearing a pair of Levi’s blue jeans, a tee and a jacket, and then I just wanted to add something, but I didn’t necessarily want the harshness of a belt,” Fox says. “I have an offcut of an old Celine dress that I’ve tailored, and I just tied that around my waist. So it just took a relatively casual outfit and turned it into something a little bit more put together.” For Byron Bay-based stylist Doria Marque, the trend epitomises her ethos of sustainability. “One of the main things that I always tell my clients, is they don’t need to own a lot of clothes, or they don’t need to buy more clothes. I really like to focus on accessories,” she says.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Fashion Week The style lesson to borrow from Nicole Kidman’s Paris Fashion Week look For those looking to dip their toe in, Marque suggests visiting an op shop and looking at their scarf and fabric section (or getting creative with a tie). “Buy a simple one before you commit, like a classic black that’s easy to wear.” Though the cummerbund is rarely seen today in traditional Indian mens or womenswear, Sindhi says a new generation of South Asian designers are “reviving and revolutionising the way traditional dress is incorporated or adapted for modern, everyday style”. As always, fashion is cyclical and Europe turning its gaze east for inspiration is nothing new.

Advertisement

In recent years, other forms of South Asian dress – like the lahenga and mirror work (shisha) – have been recontextualised by Western designers. “What’s different now is that South Asians are more visible than ever before, have more of a presence in luxury spaces and creative industries, and more cultural authority that has empowered us to ask for accountability and acknowledgement,” Sindhi says. “India is a very tempting market opportunity for many luxury brands, with its growing economic power and wealthy clientele, but what should come with that is a desire to have a dialogue that feels mutual and reciprocal.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. title: Hero? Villain? Monster? Why DC’s latest leading man keeps us guessing
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As filmmakers build new universes out of iconic comic book stories, an inevitable crossroads is reached: to continue to mine what you know, such as Batman, Aquaman and Wonder Woman, or to step into something wholly new. The latter choice is risky. It paid off for Marvel Studios, which turned Guardians of the Galaxy from a second-tier comic book line into a blue-chip movie asset. DC Studios is making a similarly bold choice in following up its iconic Superman reboot with a story from the dark depths of canon: Clayface. Perfect? Maybe not. Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures The title given to this opening chapter of DC comic-to-movie stories is “Gods and Monsters”, a sign that the franchise’s creative lead, writer/director James Gunn, intends to put a very specific spin on the screen: after Superman, in many interpretable ways as a god, we meet Clayface, at first flush, almost certainly a monster. “What James Gunn and Peter Safran are building at DC is really exciting,” says 36-year-old Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, who is playing the dual roles of Clayface and his alter-ego, actor Matt Hagen, in director James Watkins’ adaptation of the story. “The notion of being able to have different worlds that have their own identity and their own place, on merit of storytelling purely, is admirable, and I have great hope for that to continue. How it all ties together is for greater minds than mine to answer.” Clayface – whose original name was Basil Karlo – was created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger for Detective Comics #40, published in 1940, and his creative DNA came largely from the early silent film era, and the canon of early movie monsters, such as Lon Chaney’s Phantom of the Opera, and Frankenstein, played by Boris Karloff. (Basil Karlo? The homage was hidden in plain sight.)

Advertisement

Something wicked this way comes. Tom Rhys Harries in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures Kane, of course, had created Batman, and was the author of some of DC Comics’ darkest canon. True to form, the original “golden age” Clayface was a failed actor driven mad when he discovered his magnum opus, a horror film titled Dread Castle, was being remade without him. “Whilst you have an awareness, as I do, of the long history of this character and the sense of responsibility and privilege to be able to bring that into live action for the first time, at a certain point, you have to take ownership over it and tell the story that you are telling,” Harries says. “So, [screenwriter] Mike Flanagan wrote a keystone blueprint that is the story that we’re telling,” he adds. “I would grapple with that to the point where I felt like I had enough of a hold of it that then I would be able to branch off and go back and look for inspiration or anything that might inform and aid the script that Mike had written. “That might take form and shape and many different guises, and it wouldn’t necessarily have to be the comic books, but it’s something that I was aware of. I continue to feel a real sense of privilege to be part of that lineage and to be able to bring that into live action for the first time … you are having a conversation in some way, shape or form with 80 years ago.” Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in Clayface. Warner Bros Pictures At the heart of the story is Clayface’s face. Which is, at least at the beginning of the story, also Harries’ face. Until it is not. And at that point, Harries sits in a curious artistic juxtaposition: an actor, whose career is built, in many respects, off his face, playing an actor, whose face is disfigured, essentially destroying the man in the mirror.

Advertisement

“Something that felt really palpable to me on the first read of this feature was that Matt’s face is circumstantially important for what he has chosen as a profession, and the vanity of it doesn’t interest me at all,” Harries says. “It’s [more] like if a violinist lost his ability to use his hands. Or a film reviewer not [be] able to watch a film for whatever reason. “Separate to that, there’s an interesting by-product of being an actor potentially; that you then are commodified. And I don’t think it’s something that many actors that I know have a really complicated relationship with. Because it is just that. It’s a by-product of doing what my job is. “I don’t really know how I feel about it, to be completely honest,” adds Harries. “I have this sort of detachment to it. But I know that I love being able to collaboratively tell stories with people that I really believe in.” Loading In terms of building an origin story, Flanagan drew his inspiration from a two-part story from Batman: The Animated Series, titled Feat of Clay. The double episode introduced Matt Hagen’s Clayface, on television voiced by actor Ron Perlman, recasting him (slightly) as a washed-up actor dependent on a dangerous chemical to keep his face working. And notably, that television story opens with the image of the iconic masks of theatre that represent comedy and tragedy: Thalia, the Greek muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, represented by the laughing mask, and Melpomene, the muse of tragedy, represented by the weeping mask. The result is a curious contradiction: a character sprung from the superhero canon, with the footnote that he is, in essence, a super villain. But here, he has been reshaped by Flanagan, an accomplished director of horror television and cinema. Which leaves all of it in an uncertain and compelling space.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Cinema Woke but not broke? Superman soars above culture wars to dominate global box office “You’d be hard-pressed to find an individual who would be a self-proclaimed villain,” Harries says. “And I think it’s remarkable what human beings can do, and justify to themselves as actions. History is testament to that, as [are] certain things that happen in [the] present day. “To the point about the tragedy and comedy of everything, I’m constantly surprised by where humour comes from and how all of us are capable of finding the most inappropriate things or objectively wrong moments for laughter to come out of. I find that endlessly fascinating. “Part of the thing I love about him is his persistence and tenacity and strength of character that has existed way before we meet him at the beginning of this film,” Harries adds. “It’s also the thing that helps carry him over the course of the film. Whether that is expressed in the most ethical moral terms is not for me to say.” Another perspective Review What to stream this week: Josh Hartnett’s monster mystery, plus five more picks But what is left is a broken shadow of a man, whose heartbreak and rage allow him to be perhaps one of the most complex comic book characters ever written, either for the original comic book or as a cinematic adaptation. His humanity, however elusive, prevents us from wholly losing a link to him, and the possibility of a way back. “Real horror exists very close to the bone and something that is potentially deeply unsettling is when these fantastical worlds reflect real human characteristics and traits,” Harries says. “But also if you’ve had a great injustice done to you, then the response to that injustice is equal, and then the audience is judge and jury.

Pilbara miner PLS will fork out $1.9 billion after green-lighting the expansion of its Pilgangoora mine in the state’s north-west in a move that could see the operation become the world’s largest hard-rock lithium mine. The announcement is set to see the company overtake the world-famous Greenbushes mine in WA’s South West as Australia’s largest hard-rock lithium operation in terms of reserve volume, with a predicted output of two million tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate when it is fully operational in 2029. PLS produced a record 880,000 tonnes of lithium in the 2025-26 financial year. Tony McDonough According to PLS, the P2000 project expansion adds 23 per cent to the overall reserve tonnes at Pilgangoora, a larger current reserve, although at a lower grade, than at Greenbushes. The tonnage increase lifts the company’s ore reserve to 249.2 million tonnes at 1.24 per cent lithium hydroxide representing a 31 per cent increase in contained lithium.

PLS managing director and chief executive Dale Henderson said P2000 would transform the scale and competitive position of the company. “The substantial increase in Pilgangoora’s ore reserve reinforces the scale and quality of this world-class orebody and provides a strong foundation for the P2000 expansion announced today,” he said. “The maiden underground ore reserve is also a significant step in demonstrating the longer-term potential of Pilgangoora. “At 46.5 million tonnes at 1.50 per cent Li2O, it establishes a substantial higher-grade inventory beneath the existing open pits and provides further opportunity to create value over time.” Henderson said recent investments made in key infrastructure at the operation are expected to reduce operating costs, improve productivity and strengthen the existing operation, while also providing the infrastructure capacity required to support the increased scale of P2000.

The dispute will now be thrashed out in full in a New Zealand courtroom early next year. The family of a Brisbane man who died while waiting more than two hours for an ambulance despite living just blocks from a hospital found out about his death through the media. The 53-year-old man called for an ambulance after suffering chest pains on Saturday night from his home in Annerley, a short distance from the Princess Alexandra Hospital. Operators called him back at some point and asked if he could make his own way to the hospital, but he told them it would be unsafe to drive in his condition, Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said. Nicholls said the incident is unacceptable. Matt Dennien They asked him to sit tight and call if the pains got worse, but about two hours after he called, the man was found dead by paramedics.

His call had been categorised as a code 1C, which are reached within half an hour 90 per cent of the time, according to Queensland Ambulance Service data. Nicholls told reporters on the Gold Coast on Friday the man’s family had only found out about the death via media reports on Thursday night. “The family have reached out overnight, and have seen the story in the media and I think were understandably distressed about that,” he said. “I apologise to them, that has caused them distress and I understand totally if it has.” Nicholls said authorities had trouble reaching the man’s family because he was not previously known to Queensland Health, and said the family was meeting with Queensland Ambulance Service personnel on Friday afternoon.

The latest assays come from 25 diamond drillholes totalling 7121.75m at the BST1 deposit, as part of Aurum’s massive 150,000-metre diamond drilling campaign at Boundiali to test target strike and depth extensions and upgrade resource confidence. Other significant high-grade results - from three separate holes - include 1m at 43.93g/t gold from 268m downhole, 1.26m at 23.10g/t gold from a shallow 25m and 5m at 5.26g/t gold from 283m. Two additional holes also gave up 13m at 2.08g/t gold from 258m and 20m at 1.25g/t gold from 145m, including 6m going 2.29g/t gold. title: It’s the final weekend of Fringe – here’s what you shouldn’t miss
text:
Advertisement

This year’s festival has kicked off. Here, our writers take a closer look. See all stories .

CIRCUS

Na Djinang Circus | Ocker

Federation Square, until October 25 Five performers from First Nations-led company Na Djinang Circus navigate the crowd while delivering death-defying circus stunts in the middle of Fed Square. Na Djinang Circus show Ocker. Tiffany Garvie We turn back in time to a pre-colonial era as dramatic, otherworldly music plays in the background. The troupe roves through the crowd as if hunting, then gathers on a platform. The intimate audience of onlookers grows once the public realise that something is afoot. The choreography is dynamic, as the artists impressively run and tumble through people and across the stairs, doing lifts and climbing on one another. Embedding Indigenous knowledge in contemporary movements, performers emulate animals and cultural practices.

Advertisement

They cleverly introduce props – a ladder and a trolley – carrying and manoeuvring them across the flat and cobbled surfaces of the square. They mount the ladder, balancing on its rungs like a tightrope or handstand-style, then lay it on the ground like train tracks to ride the trolley over it, as if it’s a raft sailing along the Yarra River. Surprising and ever-moving, this place-based show is an exhilarating watch.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar Darby James in Little Squirt. Liv Morison CABARET

Darby James | Little Squirt

Ballarat Mechanics’ Institute, until October 24 In the depths of Melbourne’s lockdowns in 2021, Darby James clicked on a Facebook ad for sperm donation. The UK-born musical comedian premiered his one-man cabaret based on the experience at Melbourne Fringe 2023 as Spunk Daddy, and this week performed its 100th show at the same festival. Little Squirt is distinctly contemporary, wrestling with some of modern life’s heaviest dilemmas. Dressed as a seaman (say it out loud), James ponders the ethics of having biological children as a cis gay man, and what it means to have a legacy. The performer is a master of tone, somehow striking a perfect balance between ejaculation jokes and moving monologues, all with his tightly controlled vocals. The audience responds in kind, from raucous laughter to stunned silence. Tech issues on opening night mean that James is unplugged, adding an extra layer of intimacy to this already deeply intimate and thoughtful show.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

COMEDY

Creepy Boys | SLUGS

Meat Market, until October 17 This is Fringe at its purest – and this show comes with more content warnings than a film by Larry Clark. SLUGS was nominated for Best Comedy Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe last year, and rightly so. It’s delirious mayhem from Canadian artists S.E. Grummett and Sam Kruger. SLUGS is at Meat Market until October 17. Bokeh Media How often do you see the genitalia (some accompanied with googly eyes) of both performers, and see them threatening an audience member at gun-point, then offering another a very raunchy sex service that can’t be printed in these pages? Free candy is also extended to the crowd, so it’s not all R18+ (but it is 99 per cent of the time). There’s deliberately poorly performed puppetry (shout-out to a terribly voiced Joni Mitchell), and the two cosplaying as a horse. Essentially, it’s Play School on crack with a decent dollop of existential doom and dread woven in. If you’re a fan of comedic chaos with the capability of warping your mind, then I couldn’t recommend it more highly. If you prefer your comedy more middle of the road and TV friendly, then stay far, far away. SLUGS is a paradox of a show. It’s advertised as being about “nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing” but is somehow about everything. It’s breathtakingly stupid but ingeniously clever. I never want to see it again, but I also want to book again for tomorrow night.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

CABARET

Mara Knezevic | Kauboj

The Motley Bauhaus – Cabaret Stage, until October 11 In the hands of a master storyteller such as singer-songwriter Mara Knezevic, a simple tale about a Croatian man’s life and ambition becomes an enthralling and touching adventure. Two years after first staging Kauboj at Sydney Fringe Festival, the classically trained artist has brought her show to Melbourne. Kauboj by Mara Knezevic. Benjamin Draisma We hear about a chef-slash-cowboy named Jakov, who lives in the fictional Dalmatian town of Božje Selo. It’s a migrant story of hope and disillusionment. Through spoken word and song, Jakov’s world – brimming with purpose, love, fear and failure – is deftly and vividly created. Electric guitarist Daniel Potaczala strums along. Nostalgia and hints of humour are seamlessly woven in. Knezevic’s soulful, evocative vocals tackle a mix of traditional folk, covers and originals. Tender original tunes Till I See You Again and Cecilia’s Lullaby enchant, while we’re asked to sing along to an upbeat Kauboj Café and Grill. Professionalism reigns as stage lights flicker and falter and the sound plays up for a few moments. It’s a delightful hour that passes quickly.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio

Advertisement

THEATRE

In Bed With My Brother | Philosophy of the World

Meat Market, until October 3 Affectionately known as the best worst band ever, The Shaggs were a trio of young sisters from Exeter, New Hampshire, whose astonishingly inept songs were later reappraised as genius by the likes of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa. Philosophy of the World. Rona Bar & Ofek Avshalom That’s the official story, at least. Here, another trio reviews the legacy forced on three women who never wanted their spot in the limelight, but who were made to perform and record by a domineering father. In other hands, this material would lend itself to satire and condescension, but UK outfit In Bed With My Brother treats The Shaggs with respect while simultaneously trashing most conventions of respectable theatre. If you like your performances truly unpredictable, this is your ticket. Bristling with barely containable energy and randomly erupting into violence, music or comedy, the work suggests that to truly redeem artists with no aesthetic merit requires us to rewrite the rules of art itself.

★★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey

Advertisement

COMEDY

Stephanie Hare | I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy

The Motley Bauhaus – The Cellar, until October 18 From the outset, Stephanie Hare reveals their sleight of hand: physical misdirection and witticisms delivered with the gentle bemusement of someone almost surprised to find themselves delivering punchlines to an appreciative room. Adorned in a black funeral dress, the significance of which grows plainer as the show progresses, Hare moves from their sheltered, off-grid upbringing in Tasmania to a relationship that takes them to Scotland. Stephanie Hare, I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy. With a deftness that neither valorises nor romanticises a chronic illness at a time when thinness has been elevated to the pinnacle of feminised beauty, Hare traverses eating disorders, abortions and complex entanglements.

Advertisement

Hare’s tremulous voice belies a steady command of the room and their material. The subject matter is heavy, the revelations often harrowing and astonishing, but therein lies Hare’s talent. They’re exceedingly skilled at building narrative tension, drawing unexpected connections that make fun without making light, and delivering bons mots with a pin-drop precision that’ll have you simultaneously guffawing and grimacing.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair THEATRE

Hani El-Rafei | The Bruise

The Motley Bauhaus, The Cellar until October 18 What if instead of you fighting the pain, the pain was fighting you? The Bruise is Hani El-Rafei’s pain incarnate, and it turns out his pain has the form of a Victorian dandy. The Bruise is a high camp, richly intense character with a hint of buffoonery, and he takes centre stage while El-Rafei, relegated to a portrait in the corner, attempts to psychically wrestle back control of his mind and body. Hani El-Rafei in The Bruise. Through the retelling of a series of Arabian fables from his grimoire, The Bruise makes his case that pain is a worthy teacher. He asks audience members what they learned from the stories, and they are, of course, hilariously wrong. The Bruise entertains by deftly switching from the role of noble king to his jealous son, from gentle Layla to her mad lover, Majnun, and by cannily miming a menagerie of animals. It’s an accomplishment to make a show about pain safe, and wholly funny. The Bruise is the anti-hero we need to understand ourselves.

★★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu

Advertisement

THEATRE

Robbie Fieldwick | play.

Trades Hall, until October 18



Where does “play” factor in your life, now you are grown up? Has it been subsumed by sensible “adulting”, or do you still make space for unbridled creativity and connection? What even is play, anyway? In this immersive and interactive work, our energetic host reflects on a lonely childhood spent searching for a playmate, followed by a precocious young adulthood in which he discovered the “play” of theatre. Robbie Fieldwick in Play. Sarah Findlay Storytelling, theatre and physical games both new and familiar (chess, Lego, Jenga) are all employed to gently elicit answers from the audience. For Fieldwick, community is an essential ingredient, and by the end of the hour we’ve each shared something of ourselves and experienced a moment of connection with someone new. This feels neither forced nor daunting. Rather, it’s an invitation to consider the power and joy in the act of play, and a reminder that opportunities to do so are all around us every day, should we care to look and engage.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis

Advertisement

COMEDY

Anna Piper Scott feat. Margot Morales | Guillotine! or, A Modest Proposal

Festival Hub: Trades Hall - Quilt Room, until Sunday 18 October If this show’s description leaves you none the wiser as to what format it will take, there’s no easy answer. Rest assured, it’ll bring you this much closer to eating the rich. A performance lecture that debates the ethics of killing baby Hitler segues into a high-energy dance number which sees Anna Piper Scott and Margot Morales donning gauzy hazmat suits against a backdrop of capitalism’s excesses. Anna Piper Scott. Wayne Taylor The show is bedlam in a distinctly Fringe way. Scott and Morales constantly discuss their next move – the fourth wall is all but non-existent – which renders the show’s choose-your-own-adventure schtick even more fitting. Audiences are presented with three coloured folders with labelled flashcards, each symptomatic of the gradually escalating stakes of engagement.

Advertisement

You could be folded into a sketch that reimagines the exact time at which a certain propagandist is shot. You may be asked to inhabit a psychologist speaking to a comedian about the futility of employing art as “anaesthetic instead of medicine”. You might be treated to five minutes of stand-up on resisting AI. Scott reiterates throughout that she’s no longer a comedian, but her sharp asides and hilarious one-liners put paid to any doubt that she no longer is. Demonic right-hand woman Morales skulks around armed with a talent for memorisation, song and possessed dance moves. The show’s finale is Scott at her best – agitating, beseeching, elucidating – as she implores us to fight and endure.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair Death Club: A Brush with Death. Alan Robert Hopkins THEATRE

Jason Geary | Death Club: A Brush With Death

Trades Hall, until October 18



Imagine an intimate “paint and sip” session with a friendly Grim Reaper as your host. Ticket holders may bring one or two close companions into a dark, bunker-like room, which we soon learn is purgatory. I’ve brought my partner along for the ride. After learning of our untimely deaths, we’re invited to reflect on what we’ll miss most in life – then to visualise it through portraiture using crayons, textas and watercolours. If our host likes what he sees, maybe he’ll let us live. Geary as Death is both endearingly funny – he’d be right at home in What We do in the Shadows – and adept at reading the room to deliver a tailored and intimate experience. It’s an artful mix of comedy and contemplation, and I’m surprised by what the absurd exercise manages to elicit from us – both in terms of actual insight and the comically bad artworks we produced.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis

Advertisement

THEATRE

Hayley Edwards | The Carrot Show

Festival Hub: Meat Market – The Stables, until October 17 The Carrot Show is at Meat Market until October 17. Nick Robertson Staving off burnout, chronic illness and mental disquiet, Hayley Edwards is reaching outwards and within to find reasons to continue making art in a dumpster fire world. There’s their family lineage of puppeteers who’d visit hospitals to entertain sick children, which is incidentally Edwards’ very job. There’s their grandmother who finds joy in the quotidian details of the everyday. There’s their partner and creative collaborator Justin Gardam, onstage with them. And then there’s the beloved Carrot Man, Melbourne’s locally grown antidote to our dark, despairing times. A man armed with an oversized papier-mâché carrot skirting around the periphery of people’s visions to bring some unexpected joie de vivre to their day. Edwards totes their own papier-mâché carrot while dressed like one, as puppetry of incredibly ornate detail bears testament to the catharsis of creation – simultaneously functioning as a microcosm of our broader world and Edwards’ interiority. If the show occasionally veers into show-and-tell and suffers from a lack of cohesion, Edwards’ sonorous oration, natural comedic timing and beguiling manner ties it all together. Feel-good and life-affirming, the “carroting” philosophy of the show may just be the blueprint we need.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair

Advertisement

THEATRE

Liam ‘LJ’ Jumpertz | Best of Fringe Magic

Speakeasy Theatre – Apollo, until October 18 From a mind-reading giant white rabbit to an audience member’s ring reappearing in the most absurd of places, this rotating roster of magicians strikes the right balance between illusion and comedy. Featuring impressive displays of mind reading, card tricks and sleight of hand, the line-up is fun from start to finish. Best of Fringe Magic is at Speakeasy Theatre until October 18. Jayden Byrne Host Liam “LJ” Jumpertz – a talented magician in his own right – is particularly charismatic. He manages to foster an inclusive space for audience members, who he makes sure are comfortable and never pressured to participate (it’s “not that kind of magic show”, he explains). He is similarly supportive of the wider magic community, and the show provides a platform for a nice mix of established performers and newcomers. Jumpertz also pulls off some of the most remarkable tricks of the night, including a particularly memorable game of heads or tails that ended with a surprising twist.

★★★★

Reviewed by Gemma Grant

Advertisement

CABARET

Kelly Lim Harris | Yellow Fever: An Original Musical Cabaret

Trades Hall Music Room, until October 18 Yellow Fever: An Original Musical Cabaret is at Trades Hall until October 18. Maedforu The very title of this show is enough to strike fear into the heart of any Asian woman, triggering a cascade of memories of lecherous men. As Kelly Lim Harris sings in the opening number of her debut solo show: “It’s not a preference – it’s a case of yellow fever!” The New Zealand-born performer takes it further than just talking about her dating experiences, weaving literature, pop culture and cultural theory into the show, which becomes as much social analysis as personal testimony. There’s plenty of humour, but also real pain in these stories. Lim Harris’ classically trained voice especially impresses on a passage from Madame Butterfly, but is equally at home performing bombastic pop-rock originals – (Please Don’t Tell Me) I’d Be Great in Miss Saigon is a particular highlight. “We deserve to be represented with dignity beyond stereotypes,” Lim Harris says. This powerful show is not just for the Asian girlies – there’s something to learn here for everyone.

★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

WORDS AND IDEAS

Deb Robinson | In Her Footsteps: Women, Crime & Justice in Melbourne

Corner Fed Square and Swanston St, until October 18 While navigating the street-corner preachers, Hare Krishna dancers and evening hustle and bustle, podcaster and historian Deb Robinson provides a gripping guided tour about the women who have murdered and been murdered on Melbourne’s city streets. Robinson is quite the character in her bold Victorian-era hat. Many of the stories focus on victims and murderers from the 1900s: the murder of Linda Agostini, known as The Pyjama Girl; Alma Tirtschke, the victim of the Gun Alley Murder; and Jean Lee, a murderer and the last woman to be executed in Australia. Robinson delivers stories in a matter-of-fact tone with a touch of dark humour. The Laneway Theatre, until October 17 Drawing inspiration from the horror shows of the historic Grand Guignol theatre in Paris, this experimental theatre-slash-magic performance is not for the faint of heart. Darkness is Coming is at The Laneway Theatre until October 17. Lee Cohen

Advertisement

Among the lengthy list of content warnings are the simulation of murder, self-harm, suicide and violence against women. But well-known Melbourne magician Tim Ellis is a master of his craft, and is able to harness this discomfort for the audience’s enjoyment. He manages to weave close-up magic tricks into the eerie overarching narrative of the show – all without uttering a single word. The Laneway Theatre (which is in an undisclosed location, revealed upon receiving your tickets) is also part of the charm, down to the secret phrase you must utter into an intercom to gain entry. The performance at times dips into needlessly gory or overly eccentric territory, but there are enough twists that you’re constantly left wondering what’s to come.

★★★

Reviewed by Gemma Grant COMEDY

BS Productions | Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons

Trades Hall – Solidarity Hall, until October 11 A gnome, a dwarf and Elvis Presley walk into a tavern. This is all we know going into BS Productions’ Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons. The actors, it turns out, are just as clueless. Based on the popular role-playing game, this comedy show is entirely improvised. No script, no blocking, just basic character sheets and a Dungeon Master to guide the way. Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons. Yannick Douzals

Advertisement

A gang of unlikely heroes must overcome the evil usurper king and replace him with the rightful monarch. But in improv, the story ultimately doesn’t matter. Major plot points are abandoned at will, and key emotional scenes transform into sexual romps in stables. The show loses some momentum midway as characters separate, leaving fewer opportunities to riff off each other, but the ad hoc comedy and cobbled-together costumes feel endearing and deliciously awkward throughout. Whether you’re laughing at the occasional solid off-the-cuff joke or at its patchwork aesthetic, the point is you’re laughing. And that’s good enough.

★★★

Reviewed by Nell Geraets The Kentucky Meat Shower is at Meat Market until October 17. Alexandra Fimeri THEATRE

Alexandra Fimeri | The Kentucky Meat Shower

Meat Market, until October 17 Though it claims inspiration in a real event, this unhinged farce bears only the slightest resemblance to a world you or I might recognise. In 1867, a small town in Kentucky was pelted by unexplained meat from the heavens, and from that factoid playwright Alexandra Fimeri has woven a lurid spectacle of cannibalism, murder and a talking meat grinder with the face of a 16-bit video game toddler.

Advertisement

It’s a little bit Crucible and a little bit Texas Chainsaw, all delivered with Monty Python silliness and hicksploitation irony. The humour and accents are equally broad, and while the jokes are occasionally and intentionally tasteless (pun also intended), they’re served up with the kind of bonhomie that goes with good ol’ Southern hospitality. The folksy, handmade set and props crafted entirely from cardboard adds to the sense that this saga of savagery is meant not to turn the stomach but leave it pleasantly sated.

★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey Before We Begin played at Trades Hall. John Rata EXPERIMENTAL

Hamish Annan | Before We Begin

Trades Hall - Quilt Room, until October 11 If you’ve ever wanted to go on a bizarre group speed date, this is the show for you. Hamish Annan takes victims/volunteers from the audience on an escalating series of intimate interactions. Always with their consent first, of course.

Advertisement

The tasks are revealed with a ding on the screen behind Annan. SHAKE HANDS. RIZZ. UNDRESS ME WITH YOUR EYES. They all relate to dating, specifically gay dating. SWITCH. POPPERS. The promotional image of a banana with a condom on it, like Chekhov’s gun, demands to be blown. It’s a modern take on sex education, with Annan peppering tidbits about enthusiastic consent and intimacy co-ordination between tasks. The line between the sexy and the absurd is thin, and the show is at its strongest when crisscrossing over that line. The ending is a tonal shift into the serious and the personal, and one that, as Annan acknowledges, might be a bit heavy for a first date.

★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu THEATRE

Emerson Brophy | Parasocial

La Mama Courthouse, until October 11 Ex-influencer Emerson Brophy sings about the subtle manipulations of parasocial online relationships in this fun musical theatre show. Brophy rose to online fame to build his music career – the pitfalls of being an artist in the content era. Through lyrics and dialogue, Brophy shares well-studied reflections on how he and other artists, such as Taylor Swift, built a brand of relatability with their followers for personal gain. Parasocial played at La Mama Courthouse. Darren Gill

Advertisement

The tech set up is quite clever for a modest production. Live smartphone filming, equipped with a ring light, is projected onto a screen – flipping the lens on content creation. Brophy also performs an original boyband-style number alongside three different versions of himself onscreen, cleverly syncing up the harmonies. There is the occasional glitch, which is expected for a preview show, but Brophy’s affable style and improvisational flair enables him to glide past them. The music numbers are aplenty, from emotive keyboard ballads to an Irish shanty, showcasing Brophy’s versatility. I found myself waiting for that earworm, but it never quite came. Being more sparing with musical numbers, and building up to them within the dialogue, would enable more standout moments and ensure the segues feel seamless. With some refining, Parasocial has all the makings of a topical hit show – consider me influenced.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar COMEDY

Oliver Pol | Featherbrained

The Motley Bauhaus, until October 11 Featherbrained. Ash Church Did you know that birds get drunk? Neither did I. But if you notice a silly goose flying in a wobbly motion and honking at strangers minding their own business in the park, it’s mostly likely because they just got on the sauce of naturally fermented berries and fruit. It’s one of the very obscure avian insights that New Zealander Oliver Pol found when researching this show from an article in an 1881 edition of The Lyttelton Times. Alongside his other ornithic anecdotes, Featherbrained at the very least makes a solid argument that he might be the only antipodean comedian more obsessed with birds than Geraldine Hickey.

Advertisement

With manic and nervous energy, Pol pinballs through a myriad of feathered tales patchworked together with accounts from his adolescence through to adulthood. He graphically details getting botox (just not where you’d imagine injecting it), the anxiety-ridden workings of his OCD brain, his family’s history of cancer and how you can die from giving yourself a love bite. There’s also fat to be trimmed. A conversation with the crowd about pen licences meanders along, as does a poll about whether he should grow a moustache and a similarly aimless observation of Spotify playlists. Nevertheless, it’s a solid enough 45-minute debut that just needs sharper polish in its delivery and a more structured throughline rather than a torrent of tangents. But if you’re looking for an affable newcomer to start off your evening, book (book) your tickets quack snap. ★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray COMEDY

Holly Bohmer, Mario Hannah and Taylor Griffiths | Nosebleeds

The Improv Conspiracy, until October 18 Nosebleeds is at The Improv Conspiracy until October 18. Simon McCulloch and Mario Hannah The Nosebleeds, veterans of improv comedy, know it doesn’t take much to evoke the horror genre, even less to make fun of it. The trio, together for a decade, are back at Melbourne Fringe to take a proverbial (and literal) stab at the evergreen genre with an hour of uneven but charming sketches. Exorcisms become blind dates, séances turn into couples therapy, and haunted mansions turn nipples into weapons. Rather than looking to recent films, the self-described “comedian cinephiles” pull from an older vintage of horror.

Advertisement

It’s Mel Brooks via Henry James. Holly Bohmer is the perfect wide-eyed governess with no fear of her homicidal employer, Mario Hannah is the ever-likeable himbo contacting the dead to learn more about the Titanic, and Taylor Griffiths, who delivers the night’s best punchlines, is uproarious as every manservant with a handlebar moustache or ghost child. But by the fourth Victorian-era conceit or ill-formed attempt at audience engagement, the show becomes static and its parodies rote. It’s a fun night out, but it’s not quite a scream.

★★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster THEATRE

Gregory Nussen | QFWFQ

Trades Hall, until October 4 In this brave dissection of self, politics and art, Californian performer Gregory Nussen takes their cue (and title) from Italo Calvino’s metafictional work, If on a winter’s night a traveller. Centre stage is a writer’s desk piled with Calvino’s extended works, and we continue through a series of false starts as Nussen keeps attempting the play they’re “meant” to perform. QFWFQ. Sonya Katerina

Advertisement

It’s a neat framing device for their autobiographical narrative, in which the preordained script of a rigid Jewish upbringing creates visceral and lasting internal conflict for a protagonist whose sexuality and gender identity don’t stick to the script. The most powerful moments draw an elegant through line between the cognitive dissonance of war and propaganda (both historical and current), and the terrifying and complex pursuit of self-actualisation and truth in a world where, too often, two plus two continues to equal five. There is plenty to like here, but the overall result is too many references and layers – some of them heavy-handed to begin with, then unnecessarily explained – which distract from its beating heart.

★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis VISUAL ARTS and FILM

Youbi Lee | OBANG 오방

ArtPlay, until October 25 If you’re accustomed to picking up after a toddler, this interactive visual arts experience will make you feel right at home. OBANG 오방 combines the Korean term for five, O, with the word, BANG, referring to direction or room. The minimalist space is set up as a halmoni’s (grandmother’s) house, with individual stations representing the kitchen, bedroom, toilet and living room, alongside a partitioned area for the bathroom. OBANG 오방 is at ArtPlay until October 25. Darren Gill

Advertisement

Familiar household elements ignite sensory play: a mini kitchenette, a bed, a clothing line and a blow-up bath. Tactile elements feed curiosity: plastic puddle decals, a dumpling steamer, silk manchester, a straw hanging and a wooden puzzle. The experience is low stimulation, with gentle traditional music and a wall projection adding an audiovisual dimension. The space is modest, which creates a safe and contained environment, but limits the number of families that can engage simultaneously, and the amount of time you can occupy an active toddler. As you leave, respect halmoni’s home by leaving the space as you found it, which is a good lesson for the young.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar Blak Out played at Trades Hall. COMEDY

Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase

Trades Hall, until October 4 Blak Out is an ideal comedy show to see early at Fringe. It offers a range of performers delivering a taste of what they offer, leaving the audience hungry to seek them out elsewhere at the festival. The featured comedians hail from all over the country, and with a mix of four performers each night there is a satisfying variety of styles.

Advertisement

When I attended, Wiradjuri/Kamilaroi performer Jacob Keed opened with a laconic storytelling style to ease the audience in, followed by Gamilaroi comic Ben Moodie. His material skewed darker with quick jabs that met their mark. Ngarrindjeri actor/producer/comedian Kimmie Lovegrove’s personal material offered a tempting preview of the material in her solo show, which will open later in Fringe. Kamilaroi performer Cameron Ribbons, the MC for the evening and the closing act, stole the show on this night by hitting a sweet spot of storytelling and punchy jokes. His re-enactment of crocodile spotting was the perfect crescendo.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton DANCE

Weichen Cui | In Green, In White

Dancehouse, until October 3 The Chinese folk legend of Lady White Snake is forever shedding one skin for another. The most recent retellings shift the focus from White Snake’s mortal lover to her demonic servant, Green Snake, recasting the bond between mistress and maid in terms of enduring female friendship and homoerotic desire. In Green, In White. Georgia Moloney

Advertisement

Choreographer Weichen Cui explores this queer transformation in a new duet with Jiawen Feng. At first, the performers are silhouetted behind separate screens, isolated, wearing costumes informed by tradition. As if reflecting the evolution of the story, the two figures are gradually brought together – culminating in a final serpentine tangle of limbs. There are interesting moments, such as the use of waacking to playfully disrupt a fan dance. But overall, the episodic structure feels slow and over-formal, arresting the flows of desire it seeks to release. It might also be a little long – compressed to half an hour, this duet could bring its strongest moments into more volatile contact.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann DANCE

Joyce Liu | INTERLINK_SYSTEM

Dancehouse, until October 3 Joyce Liu stands before us in the gloom, a tangle of red wires trailing from one arm, fingers twitching. Finally, we get it: she is actually controlling the soundscape, summoning jackhammer bursts and ominous bass drones from a body that barely seems to move. As the noise intensifies, four creatures wake inside a plastic greenhouse behind her. They claw at its walls, tearing them open. Free at last, the juddering young humanoids – all in their underwear – begin feverishly coupling in a sort of grotesque orgy-of-Doctor-Moreau. INTERLINK_SYSTEM. Carlin Stephenson

Advertisement

Liu – also director and choreographer – builds a convincingly creepy laboratory atmosphere, with smoke and wildly sweeping lights lending urgency to the action. There’s also some irony, even comedy, in the monstrous debauch – though it does go on and on. I do think, however, we could have stayed with that opening image of the human wired for sound a little longer, perhaps giving the idea of an interlinked system more room to unfold – before rushing into the bioengineered bacchanal.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann THEATRE

Ben Grant | Wrong Way, Grow Back

La Mama Headquarters, until October 18 Wrong Way Grow Back channels long-time actor, Ben Grant’s warm-hearted charm and boyish sincerity for a part-stand up, part-confessional reflection on family lineage, memory, and grief. The title names Grant’s stop-and-start style of delivery, as he swings from mournful anecdotes about his parents’ meet-cute at Harvard to light-hearted stand up about the romance of letter-writing.

Advertisement

Ben Grant in his Melbourne Fringe Festival show Wrong Way, Grow Back. Darren Gill He’s an endearing performer. But the show lacks focus. Though the scattershot logic of Grant’s stream-of-consciousness style has an occasionally charming unpredictability (an uncanny Louis C.K. impression notwithstanding), it’s too much to ask even the most game audience to go from twee word play to sermonic political rants with nothing but the refrain “Why was I telling you this?” to justify the diversion. If there’s a chaotic appeal to Grant’s jarring transitions, it comes at the expense of the simple effectiveness of moments when he draws from his talents as a dramatic actor to deliver something closer to the intimate style of confessional or verbatim theatre: whether quietly reading from his parents’ letters to each other, or choking up when he tries to make a joke about his mum. The simplicity of these moments of quiet vulnerability stripped back the clutter to present a process of painful remembrance unique to grief, where two lines on an old letter can stop time and let you ‘grow back’. At least for a moment.

★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster COMEDY

Gill Cordiner, David Callan and Iain Pringle | 100% Scottish Comedy

Elephant and Wheelbarrow, until October 16

Advertisement

100% Scottish Comedy is at Elephant and Wheelbarrow until October 16. Brian Taylor Three Scottish stand-ups pull a decent-sized comedy-seeking crowd for a Monday night. There are 30 or more people thirsty for a laugh at the bustling inner-city pub. David Callan welcomes “Monday drinkers” before launching into a diatribe about how crappy Perth is. He seeks validation from the crowd, revealing he’s trialling new bits. While some chuckles surface, many quips and observations get the silent treatment. Next is Iain Pringle, whose attempts at an Aussie accent elicit mild mirth. Again, Perth is bagged out. After the half-way mark, he notes, “I’m definitely losing you on this”. Ramblings about working for the NDIS entertain some. Gill Cordiner’s fun crowd banter leads to light-hearted ribbing of prime targets – a bald bloke, a man wearing a hat indoors and a younger fellow with facial hair. Oddly, there’s even more rubbishing of Perth. A highly relatable dig at Melbourne’s foodie scene gets the biggest laugh of the night.

★★

Carlton are in crisis after defender Wade Derksen was busted drink driving, becoming the third Blue embroiled in an off-field issue since the end of the season. The Blues have suspended Derksen for the entire preseason and the first three games of the 2027 home and away campaign after he returned a “high-range” reading in a roadside breath test in Jabiru, in the Northern Territory in late September. Wade Derksen will miss the 2027 pre-season and the first three games. Getty Images Derksen, 25, has been charged with drink driving. The matter is scheduled to be heard in an NT court next month. The revelation comes just hours after defender Lachie Cowan was hit with a two-game ban by the AFL for conduct unbecoming following investigations of “his use of an illicit substance last weekend” by the Blues and the league.

Forward Will Hayward admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. He was not sanctioned. The Blues will start next season without two defenders from the team that bowed out in the elimination final against Geelong last month. Carlton defender Lachie Cowan. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions.”

Advertisement

Derksen had won the hearts of Blues fans by driving four days from Darwin to Melbourne for preseason training to earn a spot on the list. He was given a two-year contract extension after strong form filling in for the injured Jacob Weitering. That feelgood story now has a sour postscript. Derksen, who must complete relevant counselling as part of his sanctions, has apologised for his behaviour. Loading “I want to express how sorry I am for what I did,” Derksen said. “The choice I made to get behind the wheel that day was unacceptable and is a moment I deeply regret. Cowan apologised and thanked the medical professional who helped him after he collapsed at a party last weekend. Related Article Analysis

title: Young cricketer Ben Austin’s death ruled a tragic accident
text:

Updated NationalVictoriaCourts Young cricketer Ben Austin’s death ruled a tragic accident Bridget McArthur Updated October 16, 2026 — 1:39pm ,first published October 16, 2026 — 10:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
